Where Does Human Dignity Come From? A Letter Home Raises a Big Question
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. (Genesis 1:27)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me begin by reading you a letter home. The writer is named Hilarion, and the date is the summer of 1 BC. He is working in the great Egyptian city of Alexandria, and he is writing home to Alis.

The tone of the letter is very gentle. He greets his family, asks her to take good care of the child, says he will send money as soon as he is paid, and says, how could I ever forget you? Hearing this far, you probably think this is a decent man, working hard away from home with his heart set on his family.
The next line makes your spine go cold. He instructs: if you give birth again, keep the baby if it is a boy, and throw it out if it is a girl.

This letter was written on a piece of papyrus and dug up two thousand years later. Its catalog number is Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 744. When I first read it I stopped for a long time. What is most frightening is that the writer is nothing like a villain. When he wrote that line, he was probably about as concerned as if he were reminding her not to forget to pay the utility bills.

We shudder when we read this line today. And this is what I want to ask you today: where does that shudder come from? Why are we so sure that the baby girl who was thrown away is just as precious as her brother?
One: When people have price tags
The scale of the ancient world

We have grown used to saying that all people are equal, as if the sentence were as natural as air. But open the history books and for much of the time it was not so. Aristotle, one of the greatest minds of ancient Greece, held that some people are slaves by nature and that being ruled is actually good for them, and he put non-Greeks in that category. Brothers and sisters, this is a giant of Western philosophy.

In Greece and Rome a father’s rights could extend to disposing of his own newborn child. It was not until AD 374 that the emperor Valentinian formally legislated against infanticide. In that world, how much a person was worth depended on bloodline, sex, status and what use you were.

To be fair, the ancient world was not pitch dark. The Stoic Seneca wrote to a friend urging kindness to slaves, on the ground that they are people too. That was remarkable. But Seneca himself owned slaves, and he did not oppose slavery itself. The wall was simply too thick, and even the most conscientious people could only open a small window in it.

Let me give you a picture. There is an old gold ring. Take it to the pawnshop, and the owner puts it on the scale and says: three thousand dollars. The very same ring, which Grandma placed in her granddaughter’s palm on her deathbed: offer three million, and the granddaughter will not sell.

Did the weight of the gold change? No. What changed is whose the ring is and who has loved it. Human worth is the same question. Society holds a pawnshop scale: how much you earn, how you look, how old you are, whether you can still work. Then when a person has had a stroke, or has dementia, or was born with a severe disability, and the number on the scale drops to zero, what is he worth?
If the scale is all the answer we have, then Hilarion’s sentence is not so far away from us.
The spiritual meaning: we have a scale of our own

Brothers and sisters, we get indignant reading about the ancients, but please touch your own heart. In church, when someone in a sharp suit walks in and someone in shabby clothes walks in, is our smile just as wide? James asked the very same question long ago. That pawnshop scale did not stay in the Roman Empire. It is in our pockets, and sometimes we use it to weigh ourselves and conclude that we are worth nothing.
Two: One sentence from Genesis, and a very long road
Putting the crown on everyone’s head

Now let us look at the verse at the very beginning: “God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.” We have read it so often that we no longer feel its weight.

Many Old Testament scholars point out that in the ancient Near East, “image of God” was often a royal title. The king was God’s representative on earth, and ordinary people did not qualify. Genesis 1 takes this crown off and puts it on every human head, male and female, with no requirement of bloodline. This view is very influential in scholarship, and the details are still debated, but just picture the scene: the slave in the field holds the same title as Pharaoh.
Notice also that this passage is the Bible of the Jewish people too. Christians cannot treat this honor as our own patent.
Some saw it early, and some were slow to see it

In the fourth century there was a man named Gregory of Nyssa. He was preaching on Ecclesiastes, on the verse where Solomon buys male and female servants, and he took the pulpit to challenge it. He asked: if people are made in the image of God, who can set a price on them? If God Himself does not enslave those He created free, who dares to place his own power above God?

I would love to tell you that the whole church heard this and rose up to abolish slavery. Sadly, no. Augustine and many other church fathers accepted the hierarchy of their time, and the history of Christians owning slaves dragged on for more than a thousand years. We will speak honestly about it in the unit on abolition. The text was on the table all along, and it took us that long to be willing to live by it. This is where the church should bow its head.

Now we come to December 10, 1948. After two world wars, the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris, with 48 votes in favor, none against, and 8 abstentions. Article 1 says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

At the drafting table was Charles Malik, the delegate from Lebanon, a Christian who often quoted Aquinas. There was also the Chinese delegate Peng-chun Chang, a student of John Dewey and deeply shaped by Confucianism, who often cited Mencius and repeatedly argued that this Declaration must not reflect only Western thought. The word “conscience” in Article 1, “endowed with reason and conscience,” was proposed by Chang, and scholars see behind it the Confucian idea of ren (benevolence). As Chinese people, we can be glad to hear this.

So let us not say that human rights are an exclusively Christian product. That does not fit the history. Some scholars in recent years, such as Siedentop, argue that the Western ideas of the individual and equality can be traced from Paul all the way down, and the writer Tom Holland makes a similar observation; he describes himself as a cultural Christian. There are also critics such as Kenan Malik who remind us that the church long defended hierarchy, and that equality that truly includes everyone was hard won. This discussion is not over, and we need not hurry to declare who has won.
The spiritual meaning: those who don’t believe bear the image too

Many friends who do not believe in God work for refugees and speak up for victims, and they are braver than we are. How should we see them? We should say amen, and we should thank them. According to the Bible, they too were made in the image of God, and the conscience inside them was put there by God.
and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. (James 3:9)
Three: A firmer foundation, a higher price

What I am about to say now is philosophical and theological inference, not a historian’s conclusion, so please keep the two apart. An atheist can perfectly well defend human rights firmly, and I have no doubt of that. I am only asking this: if human dignity does not depend on ability, on usefulness, or on a majority vote, what does it stand on?

If dignity is given by social consensus, then once the consensus changes it can be taken back. The history of the twentieth century shows how dangerous that is. The Bible’s answer is that dignity is stamped by the Creator Himself, and no one can tear it off. I cannot say this proves anything. I only say that this answer deserves serious thought.
He went to the cheapest place
Here is the most moving part of the story. Who was the cheapest person in the ancient world? The slave. And the Son of God chose to go to exactly that place.
And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. (Philippians 2:6-8)

Look at these words: “who, existing in the form of God,” and then “taking the form of a servant.” The highest image in the whole universe went down of His own accord to the lowest image. From then on, there is no position so low that Christ has not been there.
The pawnshop scale tells you that you are worth three thousand dollars. The cross tells you that the One who made you redeemed you with His own life.
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)
Listen carefully: “while we were yet sinners.” It was not after you became good, or useful, or accomplished. At the very moment you liked yourself least, He had already named His price.
The spiritual meaning: from self-centered to selfless

Why do we keep reaching for the scale? Because we are self-centered. I have to be higher than you to feel safe. A person who knows he is loved in Christ has no need to stand taller by stepping on others. Let Jesus reign, and the scale can be put down. Humility does not mean thinking of yourself as worthless. Humility means placing yourself and others back in God’s hands, letting God be God and people be people.

Brothers and sisters, that baby girl of 1 BC: we do not know whether she was ever born, or what became of her. But I believe the Father in heaven knows her. When we read that letter today we shudder, and this shudder is a gift. Please do not let it fade.

This week there are three things you can do. First, follow Jesus’ example and serve someone who is of no use to you. Second, remember that people matter more than tasks: coworkers, migrant workers and the elders at home are not tools for getting things done. Third, learn the name of someone you see often but whose name you do not know, a convenience-store clerk or a building guard, ask for it, and greet him by name next time. Brothers and sisters, a name is a way of saying, “I see you.”
Please be still for a moment and ask yourself: whom has the scale in my heart weighed? And how do I use it to weigh myself?

Let us pray together: Father who created me, thank You for making me in Your image, and for showing on the cross how precious I am to You. Forgive me for looking down on those You have made, and forgive me for looking down on myself. Give me eyes to recognize Your image in every face. In the name of Jesus, amen.
1. What was your first feeling when you heard Hilarion’s letter? What kinds of unseen “abandonment” do you think still exist in society today?
2. What do you most often use to measure your own worth? If that scale were taken away, how would you see yourself?

3. Peng-chun Chang and Charles Malik held different convictions yet worked at the same table. How can we work alongside friends who do not believe for human dignity, and share our faith naturally at the same time?
“The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’ (Matthew 25:40)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Think back for a moment. When was the last time you walked into a hospital? Maybe it was taking a child to the emergency room in the middle of the night, or going with your parents to a follow-up visit. When you walked in, did anyone first ask you, “What family do you come from? What use are you to society?” Usually not. The front desk will ask for your National Health Insurance card, but no one is going to tell you to go home and wait to die because you’re just an ordinary person.

We’re so used to this that we assume the world has always been this way. In fact the idea that “there is a place set apart to take in strangers who are poor and sick and of no use to anyone” is one of the remarkable achievements of human history. Today we come to the second gallery of the Civilization Hall to see how mercy grew from one person’s kindness into an institution that opens its doors every day.

Let me be clear about one thing up front, so nobody thinks I’m here to brag: hospitals aren’t a Christian patent. In a moment I will take the contributions of other civilizations very seriously. But Christians have also walked a beautiful stretch of this road, and today we’ll look at that stretch, and at the difficulties in it.
It started with a pot of porridge

The time is the fourth century, and the place is Caesarea in Asia Minor, in the middle of today’s Turkey. The region went through a drought and then a famine. A church leader named Basil, not yet a bishop at the time, did more than call for love from the pulpit. He personally organized soup kitchens and handed out food to the poor. His sermons on that famine still survive today.

In 370, Basil became bishop of Caesarea. What he did next was to build a large complex outside the city, with lodgings for the poor, guest houses for travelers and a place to treat the sick. Even the emperor Valens donated land. His friend, a man named Gregory, compared this complex to the wonders of the world.

Think about it, friends. What are the wonders of the world? The pyramids were built for pharaohs. The temples were built for the glory of gods and emperors. And who lived inside Basil’s “wonder”? Beggars from the road, and poor people who were sick with no one to look after them. Just thinking about that contrast warms your heart. Today it is generally regarded as one of the earliest Christian hospitals established for the poor.
The logic of a blood bank

Let me use a picture to show the power of an institution. You donate a bag of blood and it can save one person, and that’s wonderful. But what if there were no blood bank? Someone has a car accident in the middle of the night. Do we wait for somebody who happens to pass by, happens to have the right blood type and happens to be kind? A blood bank stores up love, one gift at a time, so that someone you will never know can use it at the moment they need it most.

The Good Samaritan that Jesus told about is the same way. The text says: “But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion, came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.” The next day he even left money and asked the innkeeper to keep caring for the man. I often think that what Basil did was keep that inn open for good.
What this means for us spiritually: mercy has to grow bones

Brothers and sisters, being moved is precious, but the feeling passes. You hear a sermon on Sunday and you’re deeply moved; by Wednesday you’ve forgotten. For mercy to live long it has to grow bones: a rota, a budget, people regularly responsible for it. Some people feel that talking about institutions isn’t spiritual, but Basil’s complex was a sermon a shepherd wrote in the form of an institution.

Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. (Matthew 9:35-36)
2. Other people’s contributions, and our own difficulties

Now let’s talk about other civilizations. Greece had the temples of Asclepius, and stone tablets from the fourth century BC already record dozens of patients. Rome had medical facilities from about 100 BC, treating slaves, gladiators and soldiers, though scholars still have questions about how many there were. Buddhist traditions in India and Sri Lanka also have records of caring for the sick.

The one most worth mentioning is the Islamic world. Damascus already had a hospital around 706. The earliest general hospital is generally attributed to Baghdad in 805, and by the tenth century Baghdad had five more. Most of these hospitals were open to everyone, and the law even forbade driving away patients who could not pay. Friends, that is a standard many places today still can’t meet.

When we Christians hear this, what should we say? We should say: thanks be to God! If you truly believe all people are made in God’s image, you needn’t worry that others have mercy too. You ought to be glad. We don’t need to push anyone else down in order to show how good the gospel is.
The other side of the Lady with the Lamp

Next, Florence Nightingale. Many people know only the Lady with the Lamp and don’t know that at sixteen she experienced what she described as a call from God. In 1854 she took nurses to the war hospital at Scutari. In 1860 she opened a nursing school. She was also gifted at statistics, used charts to persuade officials, and was the first woman member of Britain’s Royal Statistical Society.

But I have to be honest with you: her faith wasn’t the standard answer in our textbooks. She believed all people would finally be saved, she often criticized the church, and she held that secular hospitals usually gave better care than religious ones. We can’t trim her down into an apologetics poster. That criticism of hers is actually one the church should take to heart: an institution with a cross on the wall doesn’t automatically have love.
The tension between plagues and mission

The sociologist Rodney Stark has a famous claim: in the two great plagues of 165 and 251, Christians stayed in the cities to care for the sick, fewer of them died, and more people were drawn to the faith. The claim is moving, and I like it too. But it is an inference, and ancient numbers are hard to calculate precisely, so when we tell it we should say “some scholars argue,” rather than present it as ironclad proof.

There is one more difficulty. Peter Parker, the first full-time Protestant medical missionary to China, opened an eye clinic in Canton in 1835. In its first year it treated more than two thousand people, and it later developed into Pok Tsai Hospital. He preached while he treated patients. In 1840 the clinic even closed because of the conflict between China and Britain. So those of us who come after have to ask a hard question: have our good works become tools for mission? Do we do it because we love this person, or because we want one more number?
What this means for us spiritually: loving people is itself the goal

Here is my answer. We do hope people will come to know Jesus, and there’s no need to hide that. But even if this person never believes in a whole lifetime, we will still care for them. When Jesus healed ten men and only one came back to give thanks, He did not take the sickness back and give it to the other nine. People matter more than tasks, and people aren’t numbers on our ministry reports.
3. Done to the least of these
Why would anyone care for strangers?

What follows is a reading from faith and not a conclusion of historians. Basil, Peter Parker, and in Taiwan James Maxwell, who began working in this land in 1865, with his work and his son’s later leaving behind Sin-Lau Hospital in Tainan. Why were these people willing to leave home and care for people they didn’t know?

Different people had different reasons, but one verse keeps showing up: “because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” These words are truly astonishing. Jesus didn’t say that caring for the sick is doing a good deed on His behalf. He said that person is Me. From then on, a hospital bed can be a place of worship.

Of course, many doctors and nurses today who don’t believe in God also stay up all night saving lives, and we should salute them. Still, Jesus’ words give us a reason to keep going when no one says thank you and there is no reward of any kind.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. (Isaiah 53:5)

Brothers and sisters, our Lord isn’t a doctor standing on the shore giving orders. He Himself bore wounds, and He knows what pain is. If you are sick today, I want to say this to you: being sick doesn’t mean your faith isn’t enough, and it doesn’t mean God is punishing you. The Bible doesn’t promise that every illness will get better, and some prayers have still not received the answer we hoped for. But the Bible does promise that He is here, that He has carried our pain, and that one day He Himself will wipe away every tear. If you have an ongoing physical problem, please be sure to see a doctor. Seeing a doctor doesn’t mean you lack faith.
What this means for us spiritually: from self-centered to selfless

Caring for the sick wears a person down. Long-term caregivers know this best: at first there is love, and later only tiredness is left. When that happens, don’t crush yourself with guilt. Selflessness doesn’t mean burning yourself dry. You also need to eat and sleep, and you also need to let your brothers and sisters help you. What the church really ought to do is divide this load and carry it together, and this is what we call God’s kingdom system: we are spiritual companions to one another, taking turns, with no one forgotten.

When you go home today, please do one concrete thing: visit someone who is sick, or a long-term caregiver. Or share one small load: one ride, one grocery run, two hours of watching the children. When you get there, don’t rush to give answers, and don’t rush to explain why they got sick. Sit down and stay with them. That is enough.
Please be quiet for a moment. Think of someone in a hospital bed right now, or a nurse or caregiver working the night shift, and call out that person’s name in your heart.

Let us pray together: Lord of mercy, You saw the harassed and scattered, and You were moved with compassion. Please comfort those in sickness and pain today, and strengthen those who care for them. Make my mercy more than a passing feeling, and turn it into lasting love. In the name of Jesus, amen.
1. When you or your family were in the hospital or sick, whose care do you remember most? How did that experience affect the way you see people?
2. What do you think a healthy relationship between good works and sharing the gospel looks like? Have you personally experienced a good or bad example?
3. If we turned mercy into a small institution, what regular care could our small group arrange for a sick person or caregiver near us?
The University: One Death, Three Roommates and a Crowd Who Walked Out
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction. (Proverbs 1:7)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me start with a question today: when you were a student, did you get along with your roommates? One snores in the middle of the night, one leaves socks everywhere, one sneaks your instant noodles. But however annoying he is, whatever he does, he’s not going to get you hanged.

In Oxford in the early thirteenth century, that’s just what happened. Medieval chronicles record that a student accidentally killed a woman and fled overnight. The mayor rushed with a group of men to the house he rented. They didn’t catch him, only the three roommates who shared the place. All three said they knew nothing about it and were locked up anyway. A few days later, on the orders of the English king, they were taken outside the town and hanged.

That woman, whose name we don’t know, was dead, and the three roommates were dead too. There were no winners anywhere in this affair. What happened next is even more interesting: the teachers and students of Oxford walked out together. The chronicle says three thousand left. We should take that number with a discount, but in any case Oxford was suddenly empty. Some went to Reading, and some walked to a little town on the edge of the marshes and carried on teaching there. That little town was called Cambridge.

Parents all over the world today fight to get their children into the University of Cambridge, and it started with a crowd of shaken refugee students. Friends, the university didn’t begin with marble. It began with people’s fear and a curiosity that wouldn’t give up.

In this message we’ll ask three things. How did the university come about? What is the relationship between faith and the university? And what can Christians like us learn from it today? I’ll say this up front: in this history the church has its glorious moments and also some very embarrassing ones, and I’m going to talk about both.
1. The university’s origins: a guild trying to make a living
The story of an overseas students’ association

We often say the English word “university” has something to do with the universe, which sounds very grand. In fact the Latin universitas originally meant a guild, the same sort of thing as the carpenters’ guild or the tailors’ guild.

In Bologna, Italy, a group of students from out of town ran into a big problem. Local law said that if someone from your home region owed a debt or broke the law, the city could come after you. Let me ask you: suppose you came from Malaysia to study in Taiwan, someone from your hometown skipped out on the rent, and the landlord came and seized your luggage. What would you do? Right, you would go find the other overseas students and form an association. That’s what the students in Bologna did. They organized, negotiated terms with the city together and hired teachers together. Students hiring their teachers! I suspect today’s college students would be quite envious.

While we’re here, let me bust a myth. The University of Bologna’s crest says 1088, and many people call it the oldest university in the world. That date was actually set retrospectively in the nineteenth century by a committee led by the poet Carducci, and some historians think it couldn’t be called a university until after the 1150s. Those of us who share the gospel have the least need of anyone to treat legend as history.
A papal bull and a student strike

Now look at Paris. In 1229 the teachers and students of Paris felt they had suffered injustice in the courts, and the whole university went on strike. And who stepped in to settle it? Pope Gregory IX. In 1231 he issued a bull calling Paris the mother of the sciences, allowing the university to set its own statutes and even to suspend lectures in cases of judicial injustice.

Please think about how remarkable that is. A medieval group gets a piece of paper that says you may govern yourselves, and you may say no to those in power. Today’s academic freedom certainly has many other sources, but that piece of paper really was one step along the long road.

The historian Edward Grant sees the university as the institution Western Europe used to organize and absorb new knowledge. Those theology students also had to study logic and read Aristotle, and they argued until they were red in the face. They believed the world was made by a rational God, and so it was worth studying. That’s what they believed at the time, and I’m not saying it proves anything.
Spiritual meaning: those who fear God are willing to be taught

Proverbs says the fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge. Notice the word: beginning. Fearing God doesn’t tell you to stop thinking. Fearing God tells you to admit something first: I didn’t make the world, and reality is bigger than I am. A student who truly fears God will be the most teachable person in the class, because he knows he isn’t God.
2. A story from the East: from St. John’s to the Yenching campus

We Chinese have a part in this history too. From the end of the nineteenth century into the early twentieth, mission societies founded thirteen Christian universities in China: St. John’s in Shanghai, Soochow in Suzhou, Cheeloo in Shandong, Nanking in Nanjing, and Yenching in Beijing, among others.

Yenching’s first president was John Leighton Stuart, and its motto was only nine characters in Chinese: through truth, gain freedom, in order to serve. You see, it took the Gospel of John, put it into the motto, and added three more characters at the end: in order to serve. It moves me every time I read it. The truth sets you free, and freedom exists for serving people.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. (John 8:32)

There was also Ginling Women’s College. In 1919 its first graduating class became the first women in China to receive officially recognized Bachelor of Arts degrees. Its later president, Wu Yi-fang, was the first woman in China to head a university. In those days many people still thought schooling was useless for girls.

Then came the winter of 1937. Nanjing fell, and the Japanese army carried out mass slaughter. On the Ginling campus the American missionary Minnie Vautrin, who was acting head of the college, turned the place into a refuge, and at its peak it sheltered nearly ten thousand people. Friends, a campus for study became, in the darkest of days, a way of survival for nearly ten thousand people. The school’s motto was “Abundant Life,” and they really lived it out.
There were also times they were challenged

I have to tell the other side as well. In 1925, after the May Thirtieth Massacre, teachers and students at St. John’s clashed with the administration over their patriotic stance, and a group left and founded Kwang Hua University. A school run by a foreign mission society, at the moment of a national wound, did not stand where it most should have stood. We can’t pretend that tension wasn’t there.

In 1952, during the reorganization of departments, all of these universities were dissolved and merged into other schools. If you go to see the Peking University campus today, that’s the old Yenching site. Soochow’s alumni re-established the school in Taiwan, and it’s still in Taipei today. That’s how history has come down to the present. I’m only stating these facts and leaving the judgment to you.
Spiritual meaning: those who sow don’t always see the harvest

When those teachers were running their schools, they had no idea that a few decades later the names would vanish. But the students they taught scattered everywhere to become doctors, teachers and principals. God’s work is often like this: the signboard gets taken down, and the people remain. This is the principle of life first, then relationships, then ministry.
3. The hand that locked the door: the church has also been afraid of truth

All right, now for the embarrassing part. In 1277 Bishop Tempier of Paris condemned two hundred and nineteen propositions in one go, aimed at scholars in the faculty of arts. Some have said this actually set science free, but today’s specialists no longer accept the claim that modern science began in 1277. In 1633 Galileo was convicted of being vehemently suspected of heresy. His works were banned, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest. Historians remind us that the case also involved academic and court politics, but the court that convicted him really was the church’s. Not until 1992 did a pope publicly acknowledge that the theologians of that time had been wrong.

When we share the gospel, let’s not tell our friends that Christianity has always supported scholarship. That isn’t honest, and one quick search would blow it apart. The right way to say it is this: the church raised the university, and it also tried at times to keep a tight hold on the child it raised. It’s like parents who pay for their child’s education, and when the child comes home educated and talks back, some parents want to lock the door.
And let’s not claim it’s ours alone

Here’s another matter that calls for humility. More than two hundred years before Bologna, a Muslim woman named Fatima founded the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, Morocco, and it later became an important place of learning. The Nizamiyya college in Baghdad opened as early as 1065. Did European universities learn anything from them? Scholars are still arguing about it today. China’s academies have a long tradition all their own. God has given all peoples a heart that seeks wisdom, and we don’t need to erase what others have achieved in order to thank God.
Spiritual meaning: truth doesn’t need a court to protect it

How did Jesus, who called Himself the truth, face interrogation? He stood before Pilate, and Pilate asked Him what truth was. He didn’t have Pilate arrested. He walked to the cross. Truth doesn’t need us to draw a sword to protect it. When the church uses power to crush a question, it has really forgotten who its Lord is.
Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. (1 Corinthians 1:25)

Brothers and sisters, in 1636 the Puritans of Massachusetts had not long come ashore and were still building their houses when they voted to start a college. They wrote in a pamphlet of their dread of leaving the churches an illiterate ministry once their pastors had died. Their student rules wanted students to understand that the main end of life and study was to know God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. That school was Harvard. Harvard’s early motto was once Truth for Christ and the Church, and today the one in common use is just the single word Truth. Half of its early graduates became ministers, and by the 1760s it was only about fifteen percent. I’m not out to criticize Harvard. My question is about us: why, really, do we study, take further training and earn certificates? What is the main purpose?

Today I ask you to do three things. First, take the Bible as your standard, fear God and keep a teachable heart. Second, if God has given you learning, use it to lift people up and not to step on them; the self-centered wield knowledge as a weapon, and the selfless lend it to others as a walking stick. Third, this week, find a student or a younger colleague, ask what they’ve been learning lately, and listen carefully for ten minutes without giving advice.
Please be still for a moment and ask yourself: whom is the thing I’ve learned serving right now?

Let us pray together: God who gives wisdom, You are the source of all truth. Forgive me for using knowledge as a weapon, and forgive the church for having been afraid of truth. Lord Jesus, You are the truth. Make me love You with all my heart, all my soul and all my mind, and use my mind to serve people. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. In your own schooling, which teacher changed the way you see the world? How did they do it?
2. Christian history includes both promoting and suppressing scholarship. If a friend asked you about Galileo, how would you answer honestly?
3. “Through truth, gain freedom, in order to serve”: how could those words be lived out in your present work or studies?
Abolition: The Conscience of a Generation
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. (Galatians 3:28)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! You all know how to sing “Amazing Grace,” don’t you? We sing it at funerals and at evangelistic meetings, and they even play it on bagpipes. Today I ask you to think about the man who wrote it. His name was John Newton, and he was the captain of a slave ship. And please notice this: after he came to faith, he went on sailing slave ships for several more years. On board he read the Bible and led prayers, while below deck hundreds of people were locked in chains.
Let that sit in your heart for three seconds. He loved the Lord, and he was also selling people. At that time he did not feel any conflict between the two.

Today we speak about abolition. This history leaves us with mixed feelings, because among the first to protest were the Quakers, and that very first protest was shelved by the Quakers themselves. Today we will not tell a hero story. We will talk about how the conscience of a generation was awakened, one blow at a time. This lesson has three parts: first, what the church did wrong; second, how God used people; and third, what is our turn today.
The Bible used to bind people

Over the centuries the transatlantic slave trade carried off about twelve and a half million Africans. In the holds, people were stacked like books, and when they died they were thrown into the sea. The participating nations were Christian nations, the ships were built in ports that had churches, and the money was invested by devout merchants.
In the American South it went a step further. Pastors and theology professors published thick books saying that slavery is biblical. The passages they cited are ones you and I have read.
Servants, be obedient to those who according to the flesh are your masters, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ, (Ephesians 6:5)

In 1845 the founding of the Southern Baptist Convention was linked to the dispute over slavery. In 1995 they repented publicly, and that repentance was not easy and deserves respect. But one hundred and fifty years is the lifetime of several generations.
Our Black brothers in the church

After Frederick Douglass escaped slavery, he wrote in his autobiography that some of the cruelest masters he had known were devout believers. He drew a clear line between the religion of Christ and the religion of the slaveholders, loving the former and hating the latter. Brothers and sisters, if a friend says to you today, “Your Christianity used to support slavery!”, please do not rush to defend yourself. The first thing to say is: yes, that is true, and it grieves me too. That one sentence has more power than a hundred arguments.
The spiritual meaning: the danger of reading the Bible

The first lesson this history teaches us is that a person can know the Bible very well and still use it to stamp approval on his own interests. We do it today too. A boss presses “obey” on his employees, a husband presses “submit” on his wife, and it is the same trick. If someone is being treated this way right now, if they are being abused or controlled, please know that seeking safety and help does not go against the faith.
Two: Chipping at the rock, one blow at a time

In 1688, in Germantown, Pennsylvania, four Quakers wrote out a protest. They asked: Jesus said to treat others as you would want to be treated, so would you be willing to be sold? The paper went up the line, and every level of meeting said this matter is too important and passed it on to the next level. Brothers and sisters, doesn’t this scene sound familiar? Church meetings are the same in every age and every country.

Seventy years later a tailor appeared, named Woolman. When he was asked to write wills and had to list slaves as property, he refused. He rode on horseback to meetings all over the colonies and sat down with slaveholders one household at a time. He did not scold. He just asked gently. He also refused to wear clothes dyed with dyes produced by slave labor, so he went about all in white, and his friends thought him odd. In 1776 the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting decided that those who still held slaves could not remain members. By then he had been dead four years. He never saw the result.

Then Britain. Clarkson, a Cambridge student, wrote an essay that won a prize. While riding along the road after finishing it, he could not shake it from his mind, got off his horse and sat by the roadside, and resolved to give his whole life to this cause. He went through the ports of Liverpool and Bristol, collecting handcuffs and leg irons, interviewing sailors and bringing the evidence to Parliament.

Then Wilberforce. He was a successful young Member of Parliament who came to faith around 1785 and for a time wanted to resign and become a pastor. People advised him: staying in Parliament is also God’s calling. One of those who advised him was old Newton. By then Newton had publicly repented and written an account of the truth about the slave ships. Wilberforce began bringing motions in 1789, failed again and again, and the bill finally passed in 1807. In 1833 the bill abolishing slavery reached its critical moment, and he died a few days later. Almost fifty years: one man, one cause.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? (Micah 6:8)

There was also a great crowd of nameless people. The potter Josiah Wedgwood made a medallion showing a kneeling Black man in chains, with the words around it, “Am I Not a Man and a Brother?” The medallion became a fashionable ornament of the day. Ordinary housewives had no vote, but they had shopping baskets, so they started a campaign to boycott sugar produced by slave labor and kept sugar off their tables. Brothers and sisters, that was one of the earliest consumer movements in history. You are not a Member of Parliament, but you too can be one of those who strike the rock.

Please notice that this story would be wrong if we told only about English gentlemen. Equiano wrote his autobiography, published in 1789. He himself had been sold, and he let many in Britain hear for the first time from a person who had been sold, in his own words. In 1791 the enslaved people of Haiti rose up, and in 1804 they founded a nation; France, Britain and Spain all lost out. Around Christmas of 1831, the Baptist deacon Sharpe in Jamaica led a strike that grew into a large-scale uprising, was brutally suppressed, and he was hanged. When the news reached London, it helped push Britain’s decision.

There is one more thing that must be said. In 1833 Britain paid twenty million pounds in compensation, and all of it went to the slaveholders. The people who were freed received nothing. Justice took a great step forward and also left a deep wound. Historians are still arguing whether abolition was due to the power of faith, to economic change or to the resistance of the enslaved. My view is that it was all of these.
The spiritual meaning: it counts even if you don’t see the result

The paper of four believers was shelved, Woolman died before the result, Sharpe was hanged, and Wilberforce was only a few days short. The work of God’s kingdom is often a relay like this, and you see only your own leg of it. This tells us not to lose heart.
Three: Seeds in the Bible, and us today
A strange provision in the Old Testament

The Old Testament also has a provision that stood out in the ancient world. The law codes of the ancient Near East mostly required that runaway slaves be returned, and anyone who hid them was punished. The law of Moses says this.

You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, among you, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him. (Deuteronomy 23:15-16)

Interpreters differ on how far this provision applies, and some think it refers to servants who fled from foreign lands. But in any case, the Fugitive Slave Acts of the United States, which required that runaways be sent back, stand in glaring contrast to this passage. Abolitionists used this very passage to challenge them.

So what does the Bible really think? Why didn’t the New Testament tell people to abolish slavery at once? The critics ask a fair question. We must say honestly that the Christians of the New Testament era were a small group with no power, who could not even protect their own lives, but that does not explain everything. Look at Paul’s letter to Philemon, only one chapter long. He writes to the master, Philemon, about the runaway slave Onesimus: how should you receive him?

For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while that you would have him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord. (Philemon 1:15-16)

A beloved brother. Brothers and sisters, those three words are a time bomb. How can you call him a beloved brother and also write him into the inventory of your estate? The seed was small, but it was buried in the ground. Only this seed sprouted too slowly, so slowly that it took seventeen hundred years, and that is where the church must bow its head. We can give thanks for the seed, but we may not use the seed to excuse those seventeen hundred years.

Do not think all this is past. According to a 2022 estimate by the International Labour Organization and others, about fifty million people worldwide are in modern slavery. There are foreign fishermen whose passports have been confiscated, migrant workers who cannot finish paying off their agency fees, young people lured into scam compounds, and girls forced into marriage. These things happen in Asia, where we live.
The spiritual meaning: the price has already been paid

The deepest reason is on the cross. The slave market puts a price on people, and the cross puts a price on people too, and that price is the Son of God. Christ took the form of a servant, was whipped and nailed to a cross, and rose on the third day. With His own life He tells everyone who has ever been priced: this is how much you are worth. That is why the gospel can seat master and slave at the same table.

The 321 framework says: change your mindset, change your life, change how you live. Woolman’s whole life was that sentence. This week I ask you to do two things. First, think about the caregiver or migrant worker in your company or home: do you know his name? Do you understand his situation? Second, look up the anti-trafficking organizations in your area and see how you could support them. If someone’s documents have been confiscated or they are being forced to work, please help contact the local police or the relevant labor office.

Let us pray together: Lord who sets the captives free, You heard the groans from beneath the ship’s deck, and You hear the groans today in factories and back alleys. We repent that the church once used Your word to bind people. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for taking the form of a servant and redeeming us with Your precious blood. Give us the conscience of Woolman and the endurance of Clarkson. In the name of Jesus, amen.
1. After he came to faith, Newton went on sailing slave ships for several years. Have you ever had a time when your faith contradicted some habit or business of yours and you did not notice?
2. If a friend says, “Christianity used to support slavery,” how would you respond? Try practicing your first sentence in your group.
3. When Christians a hundred years from now look back at us, what do you guess will surprise them that we treat as normal? What can we do now?
Women: The Ones Who Were Seen
Just then, his disciples came. They marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said, “What are you looking for?” or, “Why do you speak with her?” (John 4:27)

Brothers and sisters, peace to you! Let me first read you a letter from home. Two thousand years ago in Egypt, a husband named Hilarion went out to work and wrote to his pregnant wife. The letter is tender. It tells her not to worry, that he will send her his pay as soon as he gets it. Then he adds one more sentence: if it is a boy, keep it; if it is a girl, throw it out.

This letter is real. Its catalog number is Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 744, it dates from 1 BC, and it survives today. What disturbs me most is its tone. He is not angry. He has no idea that he is saying anything terrible. We should of course be careful: one letter cannot tell us how common this was. But it shows us that there was once an everyday life in the world so ordinary that this could be slipped in between the greetings and the paycheck.

Today we are going to talk about women. This is not an easy topic. Say too much, and some sisters will roll their eyes: as if the church ever treated us that way. Say too little, and we let Jesus down. So I plan to be honest about three things. First, how Jesus treated women. Second, what the church has done right and wrong in history. Third, the debates in the church today, and how we should live.
One: The astonishment at the well
John chapter 4, noon, at the well. A Samaritan woman came to draw water. Jesus asked her for a drink.

A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. The Samaritan woman therefore said to him, “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.) (John 4:7-9)

There were three walls here: the wall between peoples, the wall between the sexes, and the wall of her own life, for she had had five husbands. Notice that the Bible does not tell us why those five marriages ended. In that age it might have been death, or it might have been divorce, and in most cases the initiative was not in her hands. So when we preach, let us not rush to paint her as a bad woman. What did Jesus do here? He had a deep theological conversation with her, and in John’s Gospel it is here that He tells someone plainly for the first time that He is the Messiah.

The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming, he who is called Christ. When he has come, he will declare to us all things.” Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.” (John 4:25-26)

The disciples came back with the lunch, saw their teacher talking with a woman, and froze, but none of them dared to ask. I love this scene: a group of men standing there holding the food, their eyes about to pop out. And then? The woman left her water jar and ran back to the town, and the people of the whole town came out to see Jesus because of her words. She became the first evangelist of that town.

Luke chapter 8 records the team around Jesus: the twelve disciples, and also several women, Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Susanna and many others, who provided for them out of their own resources. Brothers and sisters, these names are on the sponsor list of Jesus’ traveling ministry. Joanna was even the wife of Herod’s household steward, which means she came from the palace. Ancient writings often do not even record women’s names, but the Gospels remember them for us clearly.

Now look at the home in Bethany. Martha was running around in the kitchen, while Mary sat at Jesus’ feet listening to His teaching. Brothers and sisters, sitting at a teacher’s feet was the disciple’s place in that age. Martha came to complain and asked the Lord to tell Mary to help her. Sisters all over the world probably understand how she felt, and I will not laugh at Martha, because she was truly tired. Jesus gently called her name twice, yet He did not send Mary back to the kitchen. He said that Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her. Many scholars think that for a rabbi to keep a place for a woman to learn was very unusual at the time. How many sisters today have only the kitchen roster in church, and no one has ever asked them what they have been reading in Scripture?
The spiritual meaning: first be seen, then be sent

The way Jesus saw women was never condescending pity. He talked doctrine with them, let them sit at His feet and learn, and treated them as disciples. If today you feel like an invisible person at home, at work and at church, please hear this: the Lord sees you.
Two: The morning of the resurrection, and the history after it

Let us jump to the most crucial morning. The male disciples were in hiding, and the women went to the tomb. According to Josephus, women were not allowed to serve as witnesses at that time. The second-century critic Celsus even sneered that the first witness was a “half-frantic woman.” If you were making up a resurrection story to be believed, would you choose women as the first witnesses? No. For this reason scholars such as Bauckham conclude that real memory is preserved here.

The disciples’ reaction was honest too. These words seemed to them to be nonsense. Brothers and sisters, by keeping that line the four Gospels wrote their own unbelief into the record. Those male disciples were great figures in church history, yet the Gospels record that at the time they would not believe their sisters.

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!” Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’” Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her. (John 20:16-18)

He called only one word, her name. Mary. This woman who had once been possessed by seven demons became the first person sent to say that she had seen the Lord. The sentence the church has passed on for two thousand years was first spoken by a woman.

After the gospel spread, change went on happening. Paul greets Phoebe the deacon, he greets Priscilla, and he greets Junia. The sociologist Stark argues that the early church held a special attraction for women, though of course that is an argument and is still debated. In modern times, by the end of the nineteenth century, in many mission societies there were more female missionaries than male. Lottie Moon of the Southern Baptists arrived in Shandong in 1873, shared her own salary with others during famine, and died in 1912 on the voyage home.

In our Chinese world, foot binding was a thousand years of pain. Around 1874 missionaries and believers in Xiamen had already started anti-foot-binding societies. In 1895 Alicia Little founded the Natural Foot Society in Shanghai; she was not a missionary but the wife of a British merchant. Reformers such as Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao also pushed hard. So let us not grab all the credit. In Taiwan, George Mackay opened the Tamsui Girls’ School in 1884, when few girls had the chance to study. His wife, Chang Tsung-ming, a local Taiwanese woman, also took part in the work of the school. In the history books she is often only a single line, but how many girls touched a book for the first time at that school?

But we cannot tell only these things. The church father Tertullian once said that woman is the devil’s gateway. Aquinas, following Aristotle’s view, saw the individual woman as a defective male, though he also held that woman belongs to God’s intention for human nature. In the early modern witch hunts, an estimated tens of thousands died, most of them women, and both Protestants and Catholics had a part. Even today there are sisters who are abused, come to their pastor, and are told: you need to pray more and submit more. Brothers and sisters, that is not biblical submission. If you are suffering violence or threats today, please put safety first: call the protection hotline, find a social worker, find someone you trust. Leaving a dangerous place is not disobedience to God. In Taiwan you can dial 113.
Three: The debate in the church today

Now we come to a topic inside the church. Can women be pastors and elders? Within evangelicalism there are two main positions, and both uphold the Bible. I will not rule between them today. The complementarians hold that men and women are equally honored but have different roles, and that the teaching and governing office of elder in the church is held by men. They value the way 1 Timothy 2 appeals to the order of creation. The egalitarians hold that gifts are not divided by sex, and neither are offices. They value Phoebe, Junia, the women prophets, and Galatians, and think that 1 Timothy addresses the particular situation in Ephesus at that time.

There are respectable people on both sides. Brothers and sisters, we may differ on this, but please do not describe the other side as not believing the Bible, or as oppressing women. We may argue over Scripture. We may not hurt people. And there is one thing both sides ought to agree on: neither side holds that women are less in the image of God.
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them. (Genesis 1:27)
The spiritual meaning: the cross of mutual submission

Now to husband and wife. When Paul writes Ephesians, he first says to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, and then says to husbands: love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her. Brothers, note that the heaviest part of this sentence is said to you. How did Christ love the church? He went to the cross. The Son of God, to save us, placed Himself in the lowest place, and then rose again. For a husband who follows Jesus, the first question is: how can I give myself up for this family today?

The 321 framework speaks of 920: every relationship is my 2, lived out selflessly, bearing the nine fruits of the Spirit. This week I ask the brothers to write a card thanking a sister specifically for something she has done. Sisters, you heard it too: the first name the risen Lord called was a woman’s. He knows your name as well. I also ask the church to do one practical thing: keep the local protection hotline and social-work resources in the church office, so that every coworker knows what the first step is when someone comes for help.

Let us pray together: Lord who sees me, You waited at a well for a woman everyone avoided, and at the tomb You called Mary by name. Thank You for dying and rising again for us. We repent for the times the church has hurt women. Heal the sisters who are wounded, protect those who are victims, and teach us to honor one another. In the name of Jesus, amen.
1. On your path of faith, which woman influenced you most? What did she do?
2. What surprised you most in how Jesus treated the Samaritan woman and Mary Magdalene? What does it remind you about how to see the overlooked people around you?
3. How can our church help sisters be seen and protected more? If someone came to us for help with domestic violence, would we know how to help?
Orphans and Children: The Hands That Reached Out to Hold the Children
But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these. (Mark 10:14)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Today I want us to read a letter from home written more than two thousand years ago. In 1 BC a worker named Hilarion was working in Alexandria, and his wife, who was pregnant, had stayed behind in their hometown. He wrote home, more or less telling his wife not to worry, that he would send his pay as soon as he got it. Then, in the same ordinary tone, he gave one instruction: if it is a boy, keep it; if it is a girl, throw it out.

Brothers and sisters, what astonished me most about this letter is the tone. He does not sound like a villain. He sounds like the sort of person near us who reminds the family to eat. The darkness of a world often does not need bad people to keep it going. It is kept going because everyone thinks it is perfectly natural.

Today we walk into the Civilization Hall’s gallery on “orphans and children.” Let me say up front: this lesson has light, with many Christians’ real sacrifices, and it has deep darkness, which is that some people harmed children in the church. I am going to speak about both. A testimony that tells only the light, your friends see through at a glance.

There is one more thing I must say first. Among those here today, or watching online, there may be some who were hurt as children, perhaps right in a church. What follows may touch your wound. You may pause at any time, go and get a glass of water, or ask someone you trust to sit with you. God will not blame you for it.
One: When a child was not yet a person
An application form not yet stamped

Today, as soon as a baby is born, the hospital writes a birth certificate, because he is already a person. The ancient Greco-Roman world was very different. When a child was born, the head of the household had the right to decide whether to accept the child. If not, the child might be put outside. We can think of it as an application form that has not been stamped, and whether it gets stamped is entirely up to the parent.

This was not merely a vulgar custom of common people. In the Politics Aristotle argued that deformed children should not be raised. Seneca was a great philosopher, and in On Anger he mentions that people drown weak or abnormal newborns, and he uses this as an example of reason rather than anger. These were the most learned people of their time.
Where did the children who were thrown out go? Some died. Some were picked up, raised and made slaves or prostitutes. When these children grew up, they might not even know who their parents were.
The strange insistence of a small group

In just such a world, a certain group of people began to look strange. An early teaching manual called the Didache, written around the end of the first century or the beginning of the second, flatly forbids killing newborn babies. In the middle of the second century the martyr Justin wrote a defense to the Roman emperor, and chapter 27 speaks of exactly this. He says that we have been taught that abandoning newborns is wicked, because abandoned children, boys and girls alike, are almost all raised for prostitution.
Notice his argument. He thought through the life that child would live in the future. This is a new way of seeing: a baby who cannot yet speak already has a future worth protecting.

I need to add a few very honest words. This insistence was not invented by Christians. Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus had long condemned abandoning infants. The church received this legacy from the arms of Jewish mothers. In AD 374 the emperor Valentinian made infanticide illegal, but once the law was passed the abandonment of infants did not simply end, and it continued in Christian societies too. So let us not say, “once Christians came, the world turned bright.” A more honest way to say it is that a seed fell into the ground, and it took many generations to grow into a tree.

They were bringing to him little children, that he should touch them, but the disciples rebuked those who were bringing them. But when Jesus saw it, he was moved with indignation and said to them, “Allow the little children to come to me! Don’t forbid them, for God’s Kingdom belongs to such as these. (Mark 10:13-14)

We know this passage so well that it is often printed on Sunday school posters with a soft picture. But look at the word the text uses: indignation. The disciples thought they were managing the teacher’s schedule: children, don’t come and bother us. Jesus lost His temper. What He saw was people keeping children out.

Brothers and sisters, there is an even more beautiful scene after that: He took the little children in His arms, laid His hands on them and blessed them. In a world that waited for the parent’s stamp, the Son of God reached out with His own hand and stamped them.
Two: Love built into a house, and the tuition paid

Fast-forward to nineteenth-century England. The streets of the industrial cities were full of unsupervised children. George Müller, a German who admitted to having stolen and lied as a young man, came to Bristol after he became a believer. In 1849 he began building orphan houses on Ashley Down. Over his lifetime he cared for 10,024 orphans.

What was most unusual was his way of working: he took no salary, did not ask anyone for funds and did not go into debt. He simply prayed, and then made his accounts public. Some at the time scolded him, saying he gave poor children too good an education and lifted them above their station. Listen to that criticism, brothers and sisters: people of that era thought poor children should stay down below. Müller insisted on teaching them to read.

In 1780 Robert Raikes, a newspaperman in Gloucester, saw poor children roaming the streets. He paid four women to teach these children on Sundays. The children worked on weekdays, and Sunday was the only day they were free. The first group was about eighty. Seven years later the whole movement had 250,000 students. The Sunday school your child attends today began as a classroom for poor children.

In 1870 Barnardo opened his first boys’ home in London. A boy was turned away because the home was full, and later died, so from 1871 Barnardo hung up a sentence: no destitute child is ever refused. By the time he died in 1905, the organization had 96 homes and was caring for more than eight and a half thousand children.

In 1895 the Irish missionary Amy Carmichael arrived in southern India. In March 1901 a seven-year-old girl named Preena ran away; she had been dedicated to serve in a temple. Amy took her in, then founded the Dohnavur Fellowship, which later sheltered more than a thousand children. We respect our friends in India. What is opposed here is the exploitation of children, and nobody’s religion is being mocked.

In 1952 the American pastor Swanson saw the orphans left by war in Korea, and what grew out of that is today’s Compassion International. In 2013 a six-country study in the Journal of Political Economy followed the children of this sponsorship program into adulthood and found that their years of schooling, completion of schooling and employment were clearly better. This was calculated from data by economists, and is no organization’s promotional flyer. Of course, some have also questioned the financial transparency of organizations like this, so when we give, we should keep our eyes open.
The wounds left by the same hands

The next part is unpleasant, but it must be told. To raise funds, Barnardo produced exaggerated before-and-after photographs, making children look worse off than they really were. From 1882 his organization sent children to Canada, more than eleven thousand by the time he died. Many were falsely told they were orphans, and there they did hard labor and were abused. The government and other charities of the time supported this policy as well, but the children’s suffering was not reduced by a single bit.

Also, today’s research tells us that large orphanages have problems in themselves. A 2020 systematic review in The Lancet Psychiatry found that institutional care is associated with poorer physical growth and poorer cognitive and attention development in children, with marked recovery after they leave the institution for a family. The Bucharest project in Romania, a randomized study, found the same: young children placed in foster families had better cognition than those who stayed in the institution, and the earlier the better.

Does this mean Müller was wrong? I don’t think so. In an age with no social welfare, orphanages were lifeboats. The lifeboat’s achievement is real, but today we know how to bring children ashore, so let us not keep them living on the lifeboat. If you want to help children today, first ask: can I help this family keep its child?
The spiritual meaning: even good intentions must repent

We may truly love the Lord and truly love children and still do things that hurt them. So love needs to listen to voices, including the voices of the children themselves and the voice of research. This is what “people matter more than tasks” means: however large the scale of a ministry, it counts for less than one child’s real circumstances.
Three: The millstone and the embrace

Now I come to the heaviest part. The John Jay report on the American Catholic Church found that from 1950 to 2002, 4,392 clergy faced credible accusations involving 10,667 minors. A French independent commission in 2021 estimated that about 216,000 children have been abused by clergy and members of religious orders since 1950. The Royal Commission in Australia also heard a great many victims’ statements.

Protestants should not hurry to breathe a sigh of relief either. In 2022 the report of an investigation commissioned by the Southern Baptist Convention itself, close to three hundred pages, found that victims were ignored and disbelieved, and that leaders, to avoid legal liability, treated complaints as confidential. A 2019 media investigation counted more than seven hundred victims. In Canada, Indigenous residential schools funded by the government and run in part by Christian churches forced more than 150,000 children to attend; the Catholic orders alone ran 66 of the 139 schools.

Brothers and sisters, harming children is already a grave sin, and even more terrible is the cover-up. The reasons for covering up often sound very spiritual: don’t shame the Lord’s name, don’t damage unity, forgive. Brothers and sisters, this uses the Lord’s name as a shield.

Whoever receives one such little child in my name receives me, but whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a huge millstone were hung around his neck and that he were sunk in the depths of the sea. (Matthew 18:5-6)

I want to say a few words to those who have been hurt. It was not your fault. Whoever the person was, however respected he was, however anointed his preaching, it was not your fault. God does not want you to stay silent for the sake of the church’s reputation, and He does not want you to hurry to forgive in order to count as spiritual. Forgiveness is a very long road. How long it takes, the Lord knows, and others may not rush you.

Please make yourself safe first. Find someone you trust, find the police, find a child protection agency, find a professional counselor. In Taiwan you can call the 113 protection hotline, and elsewhere please contact the local police or protection agency. If a child is being harmed right now, please do not handle it only inside the church; please report it. If someone tells you to “settle it privately,” you still have the right to make a report. Reporting is not a lack of love. Protecting the next child is love.
The spiritual meaning: the Father of the fatherless

The Bible says, “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.” Notice the word “defender.” God is not only a God who comforts. He also calls to account. The things that happened in the dark, with no one to speak for you, He saw them all. (The older Chinese Union Version words it as “one who vindicates.”)

God Himself also walked a road so that children might have a home. “But when the fullness of the time came, God sent out his Son, born to a woman.” The Son of God became a baby who needed to be held and fed, and who was nearly killed by a king and fled by night. Later He went to the cross, bore the sin of the world and rose on the third day. That is why we can “receive the adoption as children.” In the ancient world a child waited for the parent’s stamp. The gospel tells you that the Father in heaven has already stamped you with the blood of His Son.

This lesson brings us to a very practical place. The 321 framework says life first, then relationships, then ministry, and people matter more than tasks. For children, that sentence is very concrete: crouching down to listen to him matters far more than making the children’s program lively.

Jesus is my example: He would stop to hold a child. Letting God be God and people be people means that pastors and spiritual parents must be held accountable, and nobody should close the door and work alone. A healthy church should have a two-adults-present rule, background checks and a clear reporting process. These rules do not show a lack of trust in our brothers and sisters. They exist because we value the little ones.

This week, please ask your church whether it has a written child protection policy. If not, invite your coworkers to draw one up together. You could also begin regular sponsorship of a child, or look after a single-parent or foster family. If you have friends who do not believe, you could ask them: how do you think a society learned to treat children as “persons”?

Let us pray together: Father in heaven, You are the father of the fatherless. Comfort those who were hurt in childhood and never heard, and lead them to a safe place. If we have been silent or covered things up, forgive us and give us the courage to tell the truth. Make the church the safest place for children. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for dying and rising for us, so that we can call You Abba, Father. In the name of Jesus, amen.
