2. The stories of Müller and Barnardo have both light and shadow. What does this remind you about your own ministry? How can we do good and still be willing to be corrected?
3. How does your church or fellowship currently protect children? If someone came and told you they had been hurt, what would you say first and do first?
Writing and Literacy: Building an Alphabet for a People
Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path. (Psalm 119:105)

Brothers and sisters, peace! Let me start with a Taiwan history quiz. In what year, in what city, and in what script was Taiwan’s first printed newspaper published? The answer is 1885, in Tainan, and it was not printed in Chinese characters.

The paper was called the Taiwan Prefectural City Church News, and it was written entirely in Roman letters spelling out Taiwanese. If you could travel back in time and see a grandmother sitting at her doorstep, reading glasses on her nose, running her finger along a line of ABCs while genuine Taiwanese came out of her mouth, you would be amazed.

Why go to all that trouble? Because in those days learning Chinese characters took many years, and only families with money and leisure could afford a village school. Most farmers and women never had the chance. The Scottish missionary Thomas Barclay thought that they too had a right to read God’s word for themselves.

Today we step into the Civilization Hall and its unit on writing and literacy. We will follow one remarkable thread: wherever the gospel goes, it often begins with a dictionary and an alphabet. We will also look honestly at the shadows along that thread and at what scholars are still arguing about.
1. A whole alphabet for the sake of one book

The story begins in the fourth century. A bishop named Ulfilas, born around 311, preached to the Goths. The Goths had a language, but no writing in which a whole book could be set down. Tradition says he created a Gothic alphabet for the purpose and then translated the Bible, the earliest Bible translation in the Germanic family of languages. I should add that the Encyclopaedia Britannica warns that his life cannot be reconstructed with full certainty, which is why we say “tradition says.”

Picture the task. You want to write to a friend and discover that his language has no writing. Most people would say, “Come and learn my language.” Ulfilas went and built a skeleton for the other man’s mother tongue.

In the ninth century the ruler of Moravia asked for teachers who would instruct his people in words the Slavs could understand. Constantine, who became known as Cyril, and his older brother Methodius took up the task. They designed the Glagolitic alphabet and began translating the Gospels and liturgical books.

And the result? The loudest opposition came from German clergy, who did not approve of worship in the Slavic language. Methodius was even accused of heresy. After the brothers died, their disciples in Bulgaria developed a simpler alphabet, the one we now call Cyrillic. When you see letters on a Russian street sign, there is a line that runs back to these men who translated the Bible.
The spiritual meaning: God despises no language

Brothers and sisters, behind these stories lies a deep conviction: no language is too lowly to speak of God. In that age some thought only a few languages were holy enough. But open your Bible, and you will find that the New Testament itself was written in the Greek of the marketplace. God does not ask you to take a pronunciation class before you can talk to Him.

When this sound was heard, the multitude came together and were bewildered, because everyone heard them speaking in his own language. They were all amazed and marveled, saying to one another, “Behold, aren’t all these who speak Galileans? How do we hear, everyone in our own native language? (Acts 2:6-8)

On the very first day of the church, the first great thing the Holy Spirit did was to let everyone hear their own mother tongue. I often think that at Pentecost God had already stamped the seal on the work of translation.
2. The plowboy and the Chinese dictionary

Now to the Reformation. Luther translated the New Testament at the Wartburg, published it in 1522 and finished the whole Bible in 1534. He did not simply shut himself in a study. It is said that he visited nearby towns to listen to how ordinary people talked, so that the text would sound like human speech.

England’s William Tyndale suffered far more. Born around 1494, he translated the English New Testament directly from Greek and had it printed in Worms, Germany, in 1526. Foxe’s Book of Martyrs records that in an argument with a clergyman he said he would make a boy who drives the plow know more of Scripture than the man did. That saying comes from a later record, so “it is said” is the safer way to put it, but he certainly lived out its spirit with his whole life.

In 1535 he was arrested, and the next year at Vilvoorde he was tied to the stake, strangled and burned. Please remember one disturbing fact: the people who wanted him dead were authorities who called themselves Christians. Putting the Bible in the hands of ordinary people was once a capital crime. So the lesson here is not “the church is great.” The lesson is that God’s word is stronger than the church’s fear. In the later King James Version, roughly fifty-five to eighty-three percent of the New Testament wording preserves Tyndale’s translation. He died, but his sentences have lived on in the English-speaking world for centuries.

Now let us look at our own Chinese story. Robert Morrison reached China in 1807. At that time foreigners were not permitted to learn Chinese, so he had to study in secret. In 1813 he completed the New Testament, and the whole Bible, done together with William Milne, was printed from wooden blocks in 21 volumes in 1823.

He also compiled a Dictionary of the Chinese Language, printed in Macau from 1815 to 1823, 4,595 pages in all. It was the first two-way Chinese-English dictionary and became a model for many bilingual dictionaries afterward. Brothers and sisters, when you look up a word in an English dictionary today, there are his footprints on the road.

And how many people were baptized in his 27 years in China? Only 10. If we evaluated him the way churches measure results today, he would have been dismissed long ago. But God keeps a different set of books.

From 1890 missionaries began working toward a joint translation, and in 1919 the Chinese Union Version appeared, the very Bible many of us hold in our hands. In 1920 Zhou Zuoren predicted that vernacular translations of this kind were deeply connected to the future of China’s new literature. The Slovak sinologist Marián Gálik also believes the Union Version had no small influence on May Fourth vernacular writing, and writers such as Lu Xun, Bing Xin and Ba Jin all read it.

Still, let us not say that “the Union Version gave birth to the vernacular movement.” Vernacular novels existed in the Ming and Qing dynasties, and Hu Shih and his colleagues had plenty of resources of their own. The honest way to put it is that the Union Version was one force among several, and for many Chinese it was their first encounter with modern written vernacular.

Back to Taiwan. Barclay came to Taiwan in 1875. In 1880 James Maxwell donated a small printing press, but no one knew how to run it. So Barclay went back to Glasgow to learn printing, began printing in 1884, and the church newspaper appeared the following year. By 1913 that press had printed seven hundred thousand pages. And afterward? In 1942 the Japanese government banned the newspaper. In 1955 the government forbade evangelizing in Pe̍h-ōe-jī, and in 1969 the paper was banned again and switched to Chinese characters. Restrictions loosened slowly only after martial law ended in 1987. I am only stating facts, not commenting on politics, but the elders who fearfully kept their Bibles safe know best how precious a people’s language is.
The spiritual meaning: the Bible is my standard

Brothers and sisters, for the Bible in your hands, some went to prison, some died, and one spent a lifetime compiling a dictionary and saw only ten people baptized. So when we say “The Bible is my standard,” this book is very costly. It may be free to download on your phone, but it was never cheap.
They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading. (Nehemiah 8:8)
3. Scholars still debate, the Spirit keeps working
Did literacy really change the world?

Two economists, Becker and Woessmann, studied nineteenth-century Prussian data in 2009. They said that Protestant regions were wealthier, and that the reason was probably not the work ethic Weber described but the literacy that came from reading the Bible.

In 2012 the sociologist Robert Woodberry published a famous article in the American Political Science Review. He argued that conversionary Protestant missionaries promoted religious freedom, mass education, printing and newspapers, and that these made democracy more likely to be stable. His statistics could explain about half of the differences in democracy across Africa, Asia, Latin America and Oceania.

Christians are happy to hear that, aren’t they? Wait a moment. In 2021 Nikolova and Polansky redid the study in the British Journal of Political Science, using 26 indicators of democracy and extending the time frame to 2015 and 2016. They said the association does not hold up. So the debate is not over. If we use Woodberry’s article to “prove” that Christianity brings democracy, a friend only has to look up the other paper, and our witness is damaged.

We must also admit that missionaries were not the only force behind writing. In Korea, King Sejong created Hunminjeongeum, and he was not a Christian. Buddhists developed printing early on to spread their scriptures. The Muslim world also copied texts and founded schools for the sake of the Qur’an. God’s common grace among the nations is wide, and we need not claim all the credit.

There is another question: who decides the alphabet? Sometimes it is outsiders. Mission schools were sometimes tied to colonial education and even suppressed local languages. A translator who truly fears God asks: am I here to decide for them, or to stand beside them as they find their voice? The better translation work today puts leadership in the hands of colleagues who speak the language as their mother tongue.
The spiritual meaning: the Word became flesh

Finally, let me show you the deepest translation of all. As of August 2025, of the world’s 7,396 languages, 544, about thirty-six point eight million people, are waiting for translation to begin. God’s heart is clear: He wants every language to hear.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)

Have you ever thought that this too is a kind of translation? The eternal God translated Himself into a human being. He spoke in human language, touched lepers with human hands, and went to the cross in a human body. He did not tell us to climb up to heaven to understand God. He came down and spoke to us.

Tyndale’s blood moves us, but the blood that saves us belongs to another. Revelation says, “you were killed, and bought us for God with your blood out of every tribe, language, people, and nation.” What the passage lists is languages and peoples. The song before the throne one day will have Taiwanese in it, and Hakka, and Cantonese, and also those 544 languages that are still waiting.

Today’s application is simple. First, the Bible is my standard. Others paid so great a price, so I will read it myself every day and examine it as the Bereans did, rather than relying on what others tell me. Second, change your mindset, change your life, change your lifestyle. We read Scripture not to pile up information but to let one verse change one decision today.

Third, people matter more than tasks. Let me say this plainly: literacy is not salvation. A grandfather or grandmother at home who cannot read, an elder whose eyesight is poor, has faith no smaller than a PhD’s. We do not rank people by knowledge. Sitting with them to listen and to read together is service.

This week, please sit with an elder, a child or a new friend and read a passage from John. Read slowly and listen to their questions. If you have a friend who does not yet believe, you can ask: what was the first book that made you feel it was “speaking to me”? It could be the start of a very good conversation.

Let us pray together. God who speaks, You came to find me in words I can understand. Thank You for sending the Lord Jesus, the Word made flesh, who died and rose again for me. Thank You for the translators and copyists I will never know. Let Your word be a lamp to my feet, and help me pass this light to those who are still waiting. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. How does it feel to read Scripture or pray in your mother tongue? Does anyone in your family have a language story to share?
2. Tyndale was put to death by Christians in power. What new thoughts does this fact give you about the relationship between the church and the Bible?
3. What attitude of witness do we learn from Woodberry and the studies that challenged him? Whom do you plan to read the Bible with this week?
The Shangdi of the Ancient Chinese Books: The Face in the Old Album
Yet he didn’t leave himself without witness, in that he did good and gave you rains from the sky and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness.” (Acts 14:17)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! Have you ever leafed through your grandmother’s old photo album? I have. Once I came across a yellowed photograph of a man in a long gown standing on a field ridge, and his eyebrows and his jaw looked exactly like my father’s. I asked Grandma, “Who is this?” She put on her reading glasses, looked a long while and said, “I don’t know. Maybe your great-grandfather. Maybe the neighbor.”

Today’s message is about opening an even older album. Open the Book of Songs, nearly three thousand years old, and there is a line: “Vast is Shangdi, ruler of the people below.” Friends, those two words, Shangdi, were not written in by missionaries. They predate the birth of Jesus by several hundred years, and Paul, and every missionary who ever came to China.

We often hear friends say, “What you believe is a foreign religion.” At that moment the Christian’s heart warms, and out comes the line right away: “See, our ancestors already believed in God!” And then we add, “And did you know that the character for boat, 船, is a vessel plus eight mouths? That’s Noah’s family of eight!” The whole room applauds.

Today I am going to ask you to hold the applause. Who is in that photograph, we need to check carefully against the household registry. Some parts will move you deeply. Other parts I am going to beg you never to say again.
1. The face really is in the album

First the good news: these lines are real, and you can look them up at home. From the Greater Odes, “Huangyi”: “Majestic is Shangdi, gazing down in radiance. He surveys the four quarters, seeking the settled good of the people.” In plain words: the great God looks down on the world with majesty, watching the four quarters, wanting the people to live in peace. “Daming” writes of King Wen of Zhou: “This King Wen was careful and reverent; he served Shangdi with brightness and brought many blessings.” The phrase we use today for being careful, xiaoxin yiyi, was originally about how to serve Shangdi. Friends, next time your boss says you are careful in your work, you can thank him with real depth.

In the “Oath of Tang” in the Book of Documents, Tang of Shang says before going to war, “I fear Shangdi, and dare not fail to set it right.” I fear Shangdi and dare not fail to correct this matter. But I must say honestly here that scholars have long argued over when the chapters of the Book of Documents were written, so when we quote it, we should not treat it as a recording made on the spot of Tang himself.
These ancient people had in mind a ruler above who watches. He examines, He becomes angry, He cares whether the people are well. Friends, as you hear this, does it feel somehow familiar?
Further back: Di on the oracle bones

Further back are the divinations on Shang oracle bones. Scholars read that Di at that time could issue commands, governed wind and rain, good and bad harvests, victory and defeat in war, and also sent disasters. But strangely, there is no sign that the Shang offered sacrifice directly to Di the way they did to their ancestors. They dealt with Di through the ancestors.

At this point the album begins to blur. In 1990 the American scholar Robert Eno published a paper with a very direct title: was there a high god in Shang religion? He argued that Di may have been a collective name for a group of spirits, a generic term for some one god, or a Shang king’s honorific for his father. Other scholars disagree with him. The question is still not settled today. And let us not forget that the Shang practiced human sacrifice. We cannot cut out only the beautiful lines and pin them to the bulletin board.
The spiritual meaning: God has left no people in total darkness
So what can we say? The Bible gives us a very steady place to stand. Paul, in Athens, speaking to people who had never read the Old Testament, said:

He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwellings, that they should seek the Lord, if perhaps they might reach out for him and find him, though he is not far from each one of us. (Acts 17:26-27)

The phrase “reach out for him” carries the sense of feeling one’s way in the dark. So the farmer by the Yellow River who looked up and cried “Heaven” was not outside God’s sight. Brothers and sisters, when your great-grandfather was feeling his way, God was not far from him. That one sentence alone is enough for us to give thanks. There is no need to add anything more.
2. Missionaries argued over one word for two hundred years

We are not the only ones who found this hard. In the late Ming, Matteo Ricci arrived in China, read the ancient books and used Shangdi to refer to the God of the Bible. Later Rome grew uneasy, and in 1715 Pope Clement XI issued a decree requiring Tianzhu, the Lord of Heaven, and at the same time forbidding Chinese believers to take part in the rites for ancestors and Confucius. The Kangxi Emperor looked at that and said, fine, you don’t permit it, then neither do I, and in 1721 he banned Christian teaching.

Friends, one translated term, together with ancestral tablets, shaped the Chinese church for more than two hundred years. Only in 1939 did Rome issue a document allowing Catholics to take part in these rites.
The secret of the Bible in your hands

The Protestants did not do much better. Morrison used Shen. Later the Englishman Walter Medhurst argued for Shangdi, and the American Bishop William Boone firmly opposed it, worried that Shangdi was only one among the pagan gods. The two sides went back and forth in the periodicals, more colorfully than any online comment thread today.

How was it settled in the end? Don’t laugh when I tell you: they printed two. The Union Version to this day has a Shen edition and a Shangdi edition. Open the Bible in your hands and see which edition it is. The elders on both sides could not out-argue each other, so together they went and did something more important, which was to get the Bible translated. I admire that.
Legge, who took off his shoes

The most moving figure in all this is James Legge. He too originally used Shen, but while translating the Four Books and Five Classics in Hong Kong and talking with Chinese colleagues such as He Jinshan and Hong Rengan, he slowly changed his mind. Notice that it was Chinese co-workers who changed him. In 1852 he wrote a book arguing that Shangdi was the right translation. In 1873 he went to Beijing, climbed the Temple of Heaven and took off his shoes. He believed the Chinese had kept a memory of the true God.

Was he right? Christians still differ today. Some say it is the same One, and the gospel is a return to the faith of the ancestors; the Singapore Chinese author Chan Kei Thong argues this in a book that has been very influential. Some say it is an echo of God’s general revelation, real but incomplete. Some say the two must be kept apart, because Shangdi was later mixed up with the Daoist Jade Emperor. And some Confucian scholars remind us that the Shangdi of the ancient books governs all things but is never said to have created them. I respect each of these views, and I will not rule for you today.
The spiritual meaning: translation, a small shadow of the incarnation

But behind these quarrels I see something beautiful. These people agonized over a single word because they believed God wants to speak in words Chinese people can understand. That is exactly what God did Himself.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth. (John 1:14)
There are no eight people in the character 船

All right, I promised I would ask you for one thing. The character 船, boat. What do the dictionaries say? The Shuowen Jiezi: “a boat; from 舟, with 鉛 abbreviated as the phonetic.” The Qing scholar Duan Yucai revised it to “from 舟, with 㕣 as the phonetic.” Both accounts tell you that the piece on the right is there for the sound, and it has nothing to do with eight people.

Books like The Discovery of Genesis, which claim that Chinese characters hide Genesis, are very popular and well-meant. But reviewers point out that once you believe in advance, you see evidence everywhere. It is like lying on the grass looking at clouds: if you want to see a rabbit, the cloud becomes a rabbit. Some of those books even use modern simplified characters as evidence. How could people three thousand years ago have known simplified characters in advance?

What is more, this path was walked three hundred years ago. The French Jesuit Joachim Bouvet, at the Kangxi court, said the Book of Changes was the lost book of Enoch. Today we would not put it that way, which shows that this way of reading is no new discovery.

Friends, if you tell a friend who has studied the history of writing about the eight mouths, he will go home and check. What will he think? He will think, if these Christians are careless even about this, what about the resurrection? Our Lord’s resurrection is true, and we do not need false things to prop Him up.

Now a word about ancestor veneration. For many Chinese people this is the most painful hurdle on the way to faith. Grandpa and Grandma will ask: if you believe in Jesus, will you not burn incense for me after I die? We have to hear the fear in that question. What they fear is being forgotten.

Christians hold different practices and consciences on burning incense, and we should not condemn one another. But there is one thing we can all do: remember our ancestors better than anyone. Be the first at the tomb-sweeping, the one who knows the family stories best, the one who visited Grandpa most while he lived. The fifth commandment is to honor father and mother. It is written in the Ten Commandments and is no Chinese invention, and we can show our elders by our lives that people who follow Jesus are only more devoted.
The spiritual meaning: fulfillment, and renewal

When the gospel came to the Chinese, part of what it did was fulfill. The reverence of the ancients, and that sigh, “All have a beginning, but few see it through to the end,” find their answer in Christ. Part of it was renewal. Human sacrifice must go, and the emperor’s monopoly on sacrificing to Heaven must come down. In ancient times only the Son of Heaven could offer sacrifice at the Altar of Heaven, and ordinary people could not even find the door. But the Bible says:

God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways, has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds. (Hebrews 1:1-2)

That Ruler, high above, came down. He was born in a manger, died on a cross and rose on the third day. Today a woman selling vegetables in the market does not need to go through an emperor or wait for the winter solstice. She can bow her head and call out “Abba, Father.” This is not in three thousand years of albums. It is a brand-new page.
Response: return the album to its owner

Brothers and sisters, who exactly is in that old photograph we may not be able to settle today. But the owner of this album we have come to know. He not only remembers our ancestors, He is willing to call us His children.

From a human point of view, Chinese people believing in Jesus can look like a betrayal of their ancestors. From God’s point of view, it is a family that has wandered a long time coming home. Let Jesus reign, and hand even our people’s history to Him. The Bible is my standard, so what cannot be verified I do not say. People matter more than tasks, so this week go and visit the elder who worries that you will forget the ancestors.

Father in heaven, thank You that You have never forgotten this people. Thank You that when our ancestors were feeling their way, You were not far from them. Lord Jesus, You came down so that we may call Your Father our Father. Give us honest lips that say nothing exaggerated, and gentle hearts that honor our elders. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. Which view of the Shangdi of the ancient books and the God of the Bible do you lean toward? Why are the other views also worth respecting?
2. If you have ever said something like “the eight mouths in 船,” now that you know the etymology, how will you adjust the way you share the gospel?
3. What tensions does your family have around ancestor veneration? How can you show your elders respect in a concrete way this week?
Mackay and Missions in Taiwan: A Pair of Forceps and an Island
And how will they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the Good News of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things!” (Romans 10:15)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! Is anyone here afraid of the dentist? That is fine, there is no shame in raising your hand. Today’s dentists have anesthetic, air conditioning and television, and we are still afraid.

Now imagine Tamsui a hundred and fifty years ago. No anesthetic, no clinic. A foreigner with a big beard, in an open lot by the road, first leads everyone in a hymn, then picks up a pair of forceps and says, “Next.”

His name was Mackay. His own memoirs say that by 1895 he had personally pulled more than twenty-one thousand teeth, and his students and local co-workers had pulled about as many again. He later said that the Bible and the forceps went together.

Today we step into the Civilization Hall to see how the gospel came to the island under our feet. Let me say up front that this is not a saint’s biography. We will talk about the light and also the shadows, because a history that has been prettified is not worth believing.
1. The one who walked in: first see the pain

Let us start in the south. Many people think Mackay was first, but earlier there was a Scottish doctor named Maxwell. On June 16, 1865, he began to preach and practice medicine in Tainan, and the Presbyterian Church in Taiwan still remembers that day.

How long did his clinic last before trouble came? Twenty-three days. A rumor went around the city that this foreigner made medicine from human organs. On July 9 a crowd smashed the clinic, and he had to withdraw to Takao, today’s Kaohsiung.

Friends, what would you do if you were Maxwell? You travel thousands of miles by ship, and for saving people your shop gets smashed. If it were me, I would probably be checking return tickets. He did not leave.

Seven years later, on March 9, 1872, Mackay’s ship sailed into the mouth of the Tamsui River. He looked at the hills and the river before him, and wrote in his memoirs that a voice in his heart said, “This is the place.”

How did he begin? Quinine for those with malaria, extraction for those with toothache, then a hymn, then a sermon. That order is interesting. Think about it: if you start explaining the doctrine of salvation to someone who has not slept all night with a toothache, all he will ask is, “Could you help me with this first?”
Jesus in the Gospels walked the same way.

Jesus went about all the cities and the villages, teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Good News of the Kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion for them because they were harassed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd. (Matthew 9:35-36)
The spiritual meaning: see first, then speak

Brothers and sisters, evangelism is not reciting a speech at people. Jesus first “saw,” and only then was moved with compassion. Why can’t your coworker sleep tonight? Who is helping the child of the new immigrant sister next door with her homework? When you first see a person’s pain, your words will find someone willing to listen.
2. What remained: hospitals, schools and a skin graft that failed

In 1880 Mackay built the Mackay Clinic in Tamsui, the first Western-style medical institution in northern Taiwan. Here is a little secret: according to his memoirs, the name of the hospital was not actually taken from him. The donor was the widow of the late Captain Mackay of Detroit, who gave three thousand dollars. The two men shared a surname, which seems to be mere coincidence.

In 1882 the Oxford College was completed, funded by his neighbors back home in Oxford County, who gathered a little over six thousand dollars. That is why it is also called the Oxford College, one of the sources of today’s Aletheia University. In 1884 he opened the girls’ school. In that era, letting girls study was a novelty, and his wife, Tan Chhong-bing, a Pingpu woman, served there as dormitory matron.

Mackay’s first convert was a young scholar, Gan Chheng-hoa, who later became the first local pastor in the north. Friends, this is the thing I admire most. Hospitals move, buildings age, but he invested his life in people. When he died, the north had about sixty chapels and sixty preachers, most of them local people he had trained himself.

On Christmas Eve 1885, after the war, Mackay walked through the rain to see the ruined churches. Picture it: while others celebrated, he was soaked through, treading in the mud, visiting the ruins one by one. That day he reminded himself in his diary: everything, everything for Christ, not for money and not for fame.

In his 1888 report he wrote that the work was a mixture of joy and sorrow. I like that honest line. We sometimes describe missions like the grand finale of a television series, but he himself knew that every day was bittersweet.

In 1901 he was diagnosed with throat cancer. Friends, a man who had lived by his voice in preaching was finally ill in the throat. He refused to leave Taiwan for treatment. On June 2 he died at Tamsui and was buried there, and more than half of his fifty-seven years had been given to this island. It is recorded that among those who came to see him off were more than three hundred local gentry who were not Christians. Most of them did not believe his message, but they knew this man was sincere.

Now go south again to Changhua. In 1928 Dr. David Landsborough from Britain met a boy named Chiu Kim-iaw, his wounds festering, his fever unbroken, close to death. The wound was so large that it needed a skin graft, and in that era, where would you find skin?

Landsborough’s wife said, “Use mine.” So Landsborough cut four pieces of skin from his own wife’s leg and laid them on this Taiwanese boy’s leg. Friends, picture that operating room: the husband holding the knife, the wife lying there.

And the result? Many sermons stop here and tell everyone to applaud. But the historical record tells us that the graft failed. The skin did not take. The boy’s life, though, was saved. The Landsboroughs adopted him, and he became a pastor and served as moderator of the Presbyterian Church. He once told the Landsboroughs’ son, “Although your mother’s flesh did not grow on my leg, it is forever attached to my heart.”
This is what people later called “the love that gave its own skin.” The surgery failed. The love did not.
He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness. You were healed by his wounds. (1 Peter 2:24)
The spiritual meaning: His wounds really do work

Brothers and sisters, Mrs. Landsborough’s skin did not take, but Jesus’ wounds healed us. Human self-giving has its limits and can only serve as a signpost pointing to the greater physician. He did not send someone else to cut away flesh. He came Himself and bore it Himself. What wound do you carry inside today? The physician who has never failed is here.
3. The shadows we cannot skip: treasure in clay jars

All right, now for the hard part. If you are a friend still exploring faith, please listen to this section especially. The missionaries did not each swim over by themselves. They came in after the Qing were forced to open the ports.

In 1868, over a camphor business dispute between British merchants and the Qing authorities, British warships sailed to Tainan, marines took Anping, and a Qing official took his own life as a result. In the treaty that followed, besides camphor, there was also compensation for destroyed churches and a ban on violence against missionaries and believers.

If you were a Taiwanese person then, how would you see it? They were all foreigners, one side sailing warships and the other preaching. So we today owe the rumors and the anger of that time some understanding. During the Sino-French War of 1884, many northern chapels were destroyed and believers suffered, and these are real pains. And after Mackay returned, he demanded compensation of ten thousand Mexican silver dollars, which is also a real record.

And the hostility at the time was no small incident or two. Maxwell himself recorded six incidents against Christians in 1867 alone. The price local believers paid was often higher than the missionaries’, because the missionaries had a consul who could write letters, and they did not. Most of those names have not been preserved, but God remembers every one.

One more thing. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography writes plainly that Mackay did not get along with any of the first three co-workers who came to help him, and the mission for a time questioned whether his mind was sound. His marriage to a Pingpu woman was also much discussed at the time. And that line everyone loves to quote, “Better to burn out than to rust out,” often called his motto: we would love to know where he wrote it, but so far no source in his own hand has been found, and similar words already appear in Whitefield’s biography. It is a good line and we can use it, but let us not treat it as hard proof.
Someone may ask: Pastor, why are you tearing down our own people today? Friends, because the Bible itself is written that way. The Bible never retouches Abraham, David or Peter.
But we have this treasure in clay vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from ourselves. (2 Corinthians 4:7)
The spiritual meaning: the jar has cracks

Clay vessels means cheap earthenware pots. God puts the most precious treasure in the cheapest jars so that everyone can see at a glance that the power is not the jar’s. Mackay had a temper and his age had its problems, and still the gospel took root on this island. We do not need heroes. We have Christ.
Response: our leg of the relay

Brothers and sisters, Maxwell, Mackay, the Landsboroughs, and also Gan Chheng-hoa, Tan Chhong-bing and Chiu Kim-iaw all ran their leg of the race. The gospel on this island today was handed to us from their hands. Our calling has not changed: let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory. We are not here to worship Mackay. We are here to worship the One Mackay worshiped.

So three things today. First, Jesus is my example, so go and see the pain of the people near you. Second, people matter more than tasks, so go and nurture one person the way Mackay nurtured Gan Chheng-hoa. Third, this week please look up who the first person to preach the gospel in your area was, and tell the story to a family member.

Lord who sends servants, thank You for remembering the islands. Thank You for those who came here, and forgive the church for the times it walked beside power. Lord Jesus, You bore my wounds Yourself; make me a blessing to those around me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. The skin graft of “the love that gave its own skin” actually failed. Knowing this, what does the story mean to you differently?
2. How would you honestly explain the connection between missions and gunboats to a friend who has doubts about Christianity?
3. Who around you has a “toothache” and needs to be seen and helped first? What is one small thing you can do this week?
Hudson Taylor and the Chinese Church: A Queue and Four Graves
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. (John 12:24)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! In Shanghai a hundred and seventy years ago, a joke went around the foreign community. A young Englishman barely in his twenties shaved the front of his head, kept a queue at the back and walked the streets in Chinese clothes. The queue was not yet long enough, and they say he had to attach a piece of false hair. The foreigners shook their heads: this man is crazy. Later the team he brought was even given a nickname, the “pigtail gang.”

His name was Hudson Taylor. If you are a Chinese Christian, you have very likely heard of him, and perhaps some very moving stories. Today I will speak about him, and also about who opened the road under his feet, and then about the Chinese who took up the baton. Because if this history has only heroes in it, a friend exploring the faith will know right away that something is off.
1. Clothes can be changed, treaties cannot

On March 1, 1854, Taylor sailed into Shanghai. He was only 21, his mission had little money, and his life was hard. A few years later he simply left the society and went on his own. On June 25, 1865, on the beach at Brighton, England, he resolved to found a mission devoted to going into the interior, which he named the China Inland Mission. In 1866 he set out with 16 new co-workers aboard the Lammermuir. The rule was simple: once in China, wear Chinese clothes.

Friends, this sounds like nothing today, but in that era it was a loss of face for the British Empire. Foreigners in suits meant “I am above you.” Taylor took off that skin. What he meant was, I did not come here to make you English.
On the same sheet of paper

All right, we have been moved. Now please turn to another page. 1858, the Treaty of Tianjin. The Qing lost the Second Opium War and were forced to sign. What was in the treaty? One clause said that Christianity must not be treated as a harmful superstition, and missionaries could preach. And the same set of treaties effectively legalized the import of opium.

Brothers and sisters, imagine you are a scholar of that time. Your country has been defeated, and the other side holds in one hand a pass for the Bible and in the other a pass for opium, written in the same documents. Later a man dressed in your clothes comes and tells you Jesus loves you. What would you think?

Let me give an illustration. It is like visiting someone’s home: you take off your leather shoes and put on the host’s slippers, and the host thinks you are polite. But if you arrived in your big brother’s tank, however quickly you changed into slippers, people would still look at the vehicle outside the window.

Taylor himself opposed opium. In 1888 he moved at the London missionary conference for the complete suppression of the trade, and later testified before the British Royal Commission on Opium. We must say these things, and say them fairly. But where did his right to enter the interior come from? From the same set of treaties. Look further back: the first Protestant missionary to China, Morrison, in 1807, because the East India Company would not carry missionaries, had to go around by New York and take an American ship, and later, to be allowed to stay, was hired as the Company’s translator. You all know what that company’s relationship was to opium.

This is not to condemn them. No one chooses the age he is born into. But we cannot cut this out and not tell it. When a friend asks, “Didn’t Christianity come with the gunboats?” your answer should be: yes, there is that history, it is painful, and we can talk about it.
The spiritual meaning: He changed clothes first
who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. (Philippians 2:6-7)

Taylor’s queue is only a very small shadow. The One who truly changed clothes was Jesus. And when Jesus came, there was no tank behind Him. He had no treaty to protect Him and no consul to back Him. He Himself was nailed to a Roman cross. The person you want to reach today, what is he most afraid of? What language does he speak? Are you willing to come down from your height?
2. The grain of wheat that fell into the ground

Now I need to ask everyone to be quiet for a moment. In August 1867 his daughter Grace died near Hangzhou, at eight. In February 1870 his son Samuel died on a boat on the Yangtze. In July of the same year his wife Maria gave birth to a baby who lived only 13 days. Three days later Maria herself died of cholera, at 33.

Friends, I do not want to say anything pretty here. No golden line of faith can make something like this sound good. If anyone here today has also buried a child, all I want to say to you is: this hurts, and you do not need to pretend it does not. The Lord Jesus stood before Lazarus’s tomb and wept.

His ministry was not all praise either. In 1868 a mob in Yangzhou attacked the Inland Mission’s house, setting fire to it and looting. The British consul sent gunboats to apply pressure, and when the news reached London he was scolded instead: this man nearly brought a war on us. The following year the House of Lords even held a debate on what the value of missions really was. Some of his colleagues advised him that the mission had better be wound up.
Friends, many testimony books do not write this part. But it matters, because today we are all too afraid of being criticized.

Then came 1900 and the Boxers. The Inland Mission lost 58 adults and 21 children, the heaviest losses of any mission. In Shanxi alone, 47 of 88 workers were killed. By then Taylor was an old man, recovering in Switzerland, and the news came letter by letter. Afterward the powers demanded indemnities from the Qing court, and he chose not to accept any for the Inland Mission.

But friends, who died in the greatest numbers? Chinese believers. How many? Honestly, the statistics differ widely and no one can say. Most of them did not leave their names, and their own neighbors may even have seen them as running dogs of the foreigners. The missionaries have biographies and consuls. These people have only God to remember them. When we remember 1900, please remember them first. And one more honest thing: behind the Boxers was real popular grievance, opium, territorial cessions and the injustices of mission cases, all causes. This cannot excuse the killing, but we cannot pretend it was not there.
The spiritual meaning: the logic of the grain of wheat
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. (John 12:24)

Brothers and sisters, please listen carefully. When the Lord Jesus said this, He was speaking first of Himself. He is that grain of wheat. He died and rose on the third day, and that is why our dying is not in vain. I will not tell you that suffering is always a good investment. I will only tell you that there is a Lord who has been into the grave and come out again, and He knows where you are.
If the Chinese church were only a branch office of the missionaries, then when the missionaries all left around 1952, it should have closed down. What happened instead?

First, John Sung. A pastor’s son, a PhD in chemistry from Ohio State University in America. He went to New York to study theology, went through a fiery spiritual change that the school could not tolerate, and had him committed to a psychiatric hospital for 193 days. After he came out he returned to China, laid aside his doctoral diploma and began preaching everywhere, all the way to Southeast Asia, reaching Singapore in 1935. Many old churches in Southeast Asia today remember him from the previous generation. He lived only 42 years.

Next, Wang Mingdao. He had his own chapel in Beijing, would not take money from foreign missions and refused to join the Three-Self movement, mainly for theological reasons. He was arrested in August 1955, signed a confession under pressure, and after his release, his conscience could not rest and he publicly retracted it and was put back in prison, until 1979 or 1980. Friends, he too had his moment of weakness, which makes me respect him all the more.

And Watchman Nee. Arrested in 1952, sentenced to 15 years in 1956, not released when his term ended, and died in a labor camp in 1972. His books are still printed all over the world. The church tradition he left is also assessed differently within the Chinese church.
Two paths and an honest number

Christians in China today include those who meet in registered churches and those who meet in house churches. There is complicated history and differing conscience here, and those of us abroad are in no position to point from a distance. Both sides have real believers, and both sides have their costs.

And the numbers? You may have heard the figure of one hundred million. The Pew Research Center summarized in 2023: the official white paper says 38 million Protestants, academic surveys show about two percent of adults calling themselves Christian, some Christian research bodies estimate seven to nine percent, and the surveys may undercount. Pew’s judgment is that growth seems to have leveled off. Friends, to share the gospel we do not need a figure whose source cannot be found.

The gospel also followed the migrants. In Singapore’s 2020 census, about 21.6 percent of Chinese residents were Christian. Malaysia and Indonesia both have deep-rooted Chinese churches. And New Zealand? Let me give you a name: Alexander Don. In 1879 he began preaching to the Chinese gold miners of Otago, traveling through the mining districts every year and visiting in Cantonese. In 34 years he baptized about 20 people.

Twenty! By today’s KPIs he would have been fired long ago. But he left a bilingual register of the Chinese, recording these exiles one by one, and it has become a precious source for studying Chinese history in New Zealand today. In an age when Chinese were charged a poll tax, someone wrote their names down one by one. That in itself is the gospel.
The spiritual meaning: only God who gives the increase
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. (1 Corinthians 3:6-7)
Response: to whom is your link joined?

Brothers and sisters, when Taylor died in 1905, the Inland Mission had 825 members. Those numbers are all gone today, and so are the people. What remains is a chain: from Liang Fa, John Sung and Wang Mingdao, link after link, to the one who led you to Christ, and then to you.

So today’s call is simple. Jesus is my example, so go and put on a friend’s slippers. Live out selflessness and hand over to the Lord that grain of wheat you are gripping so tightly. And in 235 spiritual companions: your link, to whom is it joined now? Please think of one name. Let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory, for we are only those who plant and water.

Lord Jesus, You are the grain of wheat that fell into the ground. Thank You, and thank You for those who carried the gospel to the Chinese. Forgive them and us for walking beside power. Comfort everyone who stands beside a grave, remember the brothers and sisters who are still suffering for You today, and make me willing to fall as one grain. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. How did you feel about the slippers and the tank? How would you answer a friend who says, “Christianity came with the gunboats”?
2. Wang Mingdao signed a confession and then publicly retracted it. Is the weakness of a spiritual forebear a stumbling block to you, or a comfort?
3. Alexander Don baptized about 20 people in 34 years. Where in your service do the numbers not look good? How does this story help you?
The Church’s Dark History: A Ledger That Does Not Defend Itself
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. (1 John 1:9)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace! When you share the gospel, has anyone ever asked you, “Haven’t you Christians killed people too? The Crusades, the witch burnings, and those news stories about priests?” Sometimes the person asking is angry, and sometimes they have truly been hurt.

How fast did your heart beat at that moment? Most people react in one of two ways. The first is to be a lawyer: “Those weren’t real Christians,” “That was the Catholics,” “That was the Middle Ages,” “Atheists have killed people too.” The second is to look down: “Yes, yes, we’re terrible,” and then change the subject quickly.

In today’s lesson I want to take a third road: open the ledger and read it line by line. Admit what must be admitted, correct what is exaggerated, and then show how Jesus Himself reads this ledger. The first ten units of the Civilization Hall speak of the good the gospel has brought; without today’s lesson, none of that would be worth believing.
1. The ledger is opened: admit first what must be admitted

Let me start with one scene. In the spring of 1096, the First Crusade set out. They were going thousands of kilometers to rescue the Holy Land, and then some said, why go so far, when the “enemies” of Christ live right next door? So in Worms at least eight hundred Jews were killed, and in Mainz at least eleven hundred.

Some bishops did try to protect the Jews. The archbishop of Mainz took people into his own palace, and the column broke in and killed them anyway. The bishop of Worms had the same experience. The bishop of Speyer managed to save many. There were condemnations from church leaders as well. But, friends, the families of the victims did not come back to life because someone condemned it. The killers had been baptized.

In 1099 the Crusaders took Jerusalem, and there was a massacre in the city. In 1204 the Fourth Crusade broke into Constantinople, a Christian city. Some eight hundred years later, Pope John Paul II told the Orthodox Patriarch Bartholomew that after eight centuries, how could he not share the Patriarch’s revulsion and pain?

The Spanish Inquisition lasted more than three hundred years. It used torture to extract confessions and public executions to create terror, and its target was often forced converts from Judaism and the descendants of Muslims. In the witch hunts of Europe, roughly thirty to sixty thousand people were executed, mostly women, in both Catholic and Protestant regions. Protestants should not think this has nothing to do with them: in 1543 Luther wrote extremely vicious anti-Jewish writings. In 1994 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America formally repudiated those writings, and also admitted that the Holocaust took place where Lutheran churches had flourished, and that they carry a special burden.

In 1455 a bull of Pope Nicholas V permitted the Portuguese king to conquer non-Christians. Documents of this kind later became the basis of the “Doctrine of Discovery,” used to justify seizing Indigenous lands. Only in 2023 did the Vatican formally declare that it is not part of Catholic teaching.

In the United States, the Southern Baptist Convention was at first bound up with slavery. In 1995, at Atlanta, they passed a resolution admitting that many early leaders defended the right to hold slaves, and apologizing to African Americans. We should know that at that time there were people who quoted the Bible with one hand and defended slavery with the other.

In Canada’s Indigenous residential schools, more than a hundred and fifty thousand children were forced from their homes into government-funded Christian schools, their languages suppressed and their families broken. In 2022 the pope said in Canada, “I am sorry.” As for contemporary child sexual abuse and its cover-up, we covered that in Unit 6; it is today’s matter, not ancient history.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter into the Kingdom of Heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’ (Matthew 7:21-23)
The spiritual meaning: do not rush to say “that wasn’t us”

Brothers and sisters, we badly want to say that those people were not real Christians. Perhaps some indeed were not. Jesus said He will sort that out Himself. But the words should not come hastily from our mouths. That is the Lord’s right to judge. Our duty is simpler: to admit that this happened in our own house.
2. Checking the numbers: no exaggeration, and no escape

So may we correct exaggerated claims? We may, and we should. The truth itself pleases God, and when others exaggerate, whether it helps us or hurts us, we must tell the truth. But we must be careful that correcting numbers does not become a way to get off the hook. Here is an illustration. A doctor is found to have prescribed the wrong medicine for years. We may argue over how many people he harmed, and we should find out; but whatever the number, it can never serve as evidence that he is innocent.

First, the witch hunts. On the internet you often see “nine million witches burned,” and historians have refuted that number. Modern estimates are about thirty to sixty thousand. And many people do not know that most of the sentences came from secular courts and local authorities. In Spain, Portugal and Italy, where the Inquisition held power, large-scale witch hunts were actually restrained. In the 1610s the Spanish inquisitor Salazar investigated and ended the witch hunt in the Basque region.

Next, the Spanish Inquisition. In the nineteenth century Llorente said more than thirty thousand were executed. Scholars who later examined the archives found a very different picture. Contreras and Henningsen counted about forty-four thousand trials from 1540 to 1700, with 826 actually executed. Kamen thinks the whole period did not exceed three thousand, and some scholars estimate close to or slightly under ten thousand. Methods differ and the archives have gaps, so it is best to say “thousands” rather than quote one precise number.

The Jerusalem massacre of 1099 has also been re-examined by scholars. Hirschler studied the Arabic sources and concluded that the early sources show that killing did occur, but that the narrative of a total massacre of the city took shape later. Kedar traced in detail the accounts of the Western historians. The killing certainly happened; its scale is still being studied.

Please remember: of three thousand lives, not one is an “only.” The secular judges who sentenced witches to death also went to church, and the demonology they believed was inseparable from the preaching. So after correcting the numbers, our conclusion is not “well, that’s not so bad.” Our conclusion is: now we know more accurately, and sin is still sin.

History has another, thinner thread. In 1146, when Bernard was recruiting for the Second Crusade, he condemned attacks on Jews, although his own views of the Jews were also prejudiced. In 1550 the Dominican friar Las Casas debated the scholar Sepúlveda at Valladolid. Sepúlveda cited Aristotle to say the Indians were natural slaves, and Las Casas refuted him. Sadly, after the debate, conquest and cruelty went on.

I mention these not to offset anything. A hundred good people cannot offset one murdered child. I mention them because when they condemned these atrocities, they used Jesus’ own words. Part of how we know the Crusades were wrong is that we have read the Sermon on the Mount.

Oh, Lord, the great and dreadful God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments, we have sinned, and have dealt perversely, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even turning aside from your precepts and from your ordinances. (Daniel 9:4-5)

Daniel is almost the one figure in the Bible with no stain. Yet the word he used in prayer was “we.” He had not personally committed his ancestors’ sins, but he stood inside them. This is the best posture for facing church history: not “they,” but “we.” On March 12, 2000, the Holy See held a Day of Pardon, confessing sins committed in defense of the truth, sins against Israel, and sins against the dignity of women. Protestants need not agree with all Catholic theology, but we can learn this posture.
3. Jesus did not fail; His followers did

Now I will say the strongest thing on behalf of the critics. They say: you keep saying “those people went against Jesus,” but what about the good? Hospitals, universities, abolition, you say these are all the credit of the faith. The good goes to my account and the bad to someone else’s; how could that ever be refuted?

Friends, that challenge is fair, and I do not have a perfect answer. I can say only two things. First, the Bible never said that a Christian society would be a nation of good people. It says people are sinners, that wheat and weeds grow together, and that judgment begins with the household of God. Second, I do not want you to believe in the church. I want you to look at Jesus.

Who crucified Jesus? Not atheists. It was the most devout religious leaders of the day, together with Roman political power, together with a crowd that days earlier had shouted His welcome. So the cross is long since the most thorough indictment of religious violence.

When Peter drew his sword, Jesus said, “Put your sword back into its place, for all those who take the sword will die by the sword.” When James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven, Jesus turned and rebuked them. When Pilate questioned Him, He said, “My Kingdom is not of this world.” The sword in the Crusaders’ hands, Jesus had told people to put away in Gethsemane.
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34)
The spiritual meaning: the only way out

This prayer is our hope. If salvation depended on the church’s report card, we would all fail. But the gospel says, “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” He prayed for those who nailed Him, prepared a way of repentance for the killing Crusaders, and for you and me. He rose on the third day, so the last word of history is not the church’s failure but His grace and His judgment.

I also want to say to friends who have been hurt by the church: your anger is justified. You do not have to forgive the church first in order to believe in Jesus. If you are being harmed right now, please find safety first and find professional help. Jesus is on your side; He too was once a victim of religious violence.

There is a line in the 321 framework: humility overcomes pride. You do not have to be a lawyer for two thousand years of church history. The next time a friend asks you, you can say, “Yes, that’s true, and I’m grieved too.” You will find that the conversation opens up instead. Let Jesus reign: the Crusades and the Inquisition both said they were for the Lord, but in fact they were grasping power. Leaving one’s place to grasp power is the greatest form of self-centeredness.

True repentance bears fruit. Zacchaeus said to the Lord, “If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much.” Disciples of Jesus should not be content with an apology without restitution. The church today must ask itself: have we made restitution? Have we handed over power? Have we accepted that others may not forgive immediately?

This week, if you know someone who has been hurt by the church or by Christians, ask: “Would you be willing to tell me what happened?” Then just listen, without defending. You can also ask a friend who does not yet believe: what is the thing the church has done that disappointed you most? I would like to hear your thoughts.

Let us pray together. Righteous Lord, we have sinned, and our ancestors and the church have sinned too. Have mercy on those harmed in the name of the cross; You remember all their tears. Do not let us make excuses for ourselves. Thank You, Lord Jesus, for dying on the cross for sinners and rising to give us new life; make us bear fruit that fits repentance. In Jesus’ name, amen.
1. When a friend asks, “Haven’t Christians killed people too?” how have you usually answered? What does today’s lesson make you want to change?
2. Where is the line between correcting exaggerated numbers and defending the crimes? Please discuss one example.
3. Daniel confessed using “we.” Is there anything in our church, family or culture where we need to stand inside and confess in this way? What would the concrete fruit be?
The Great Revival at the End: A Hope Without a Date

‘It will be in the last days, says God, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your young men will see visions. Your old men will dream dreams. (Acts 2:17)

Brothers and sisters, peace! The Civilization Hall has come to its last stop. Let me show you two numbers first. In 1900 Africa had about nine million six hundred thousand Christians. In 2025 it had about seven hundred and fifty million. Friends, that is a growth of nearly eighty times in less than two lifetimes.

If you had asked a British missionary in 1900 to predict where most of the world’s Christians would be today, he would most likely have said, “Europe and America, of course.” He would be so astonished he would drop his teacup.

Today’s lesson is called “The Great Revival at the End.” It is a topic that is easy to take too far. So let me draw three lines first. First, I will not tell you what day revival will come or what year the Lord will return. Second, we will check the numbers, the good and the bad. Third, evangelicals hold different views on the end times; we will set them side by side and not rule between them. Let us bring hope, and bring sober-mindedness too.

In its 2025 statistics, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity says that in 1900 only 17.6 percent of the world’s Christians lived in the Global South, meaning regions such as Africa, Asia, Latin America and Oceania. In 2025 it was nearly 69 percent. They project 78 percent by 2050.

Look at the continents: Africa from under ten million to seven hundred and fifty million. Asia from twenty-two million to over four hundred million. Latin America from sixty-two million to six hundred and twenty million. When the American historian Philip Jenkins wrote The Next Christendom in 2002, he was already warning Western churches that what they could see was not the whole picture.

This is like a river changing course. People standing by the old channel see less and less water and think the river is drying up; people who walk to the new channel see a flood. Today’s typical Christian may be a mother in Nigeria or a young person in Brazil, not an old gentleman in a European church.
Looking at the cold side too

But I cannot report only good news. A 2025 Pew Research Center report says that from 2010 to 2020 the world’s Christians grew from 2.1 billion to 2.3 billion, but their share of the world’s population fell from 31 percent to 29 percent. Why? One important reason is that many people who grew up in Christian homes left the faith as adults.

Christians in Australia have fallen to slightly under half. Europe’s Christians have fallen by 9 percent. Brothers and sisters here from New Zealand, Singapore and Malaysia probably feel something about this in your own hearts. So “great revival” and “great loss” are both happening at once. An honest speaker must tell you both.

Also, Pew says 2.3 billion, while the Center for the Study of Global Christianity’s 2026 statistics say 2.6 billion, a difference of several hundred million, because the definitions and methods differ. As for how many Christians there are in China, estimates differ enormously. When you pass numbers on, please be careful. When you see a startling figure, first ask: who counted it? How?

After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, dressed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands. They cried with a loud voice, saying, “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:9-10)
The spiritual meaning: God’s territory is bigger than my church

Sometimes we feel the church is in decline because the church near our home has grown old. But the crowd John saw in the vision was one “which no man could count.” The statisticians’ numbers may be argued over, but John’s sentence rescues the statisticians.

From God’s point of view, from heaven’s and eternity’s, my small church is only a small window. This humbles me, and it lifts me up. But let me be clear: to say these trends are God’s work is an interpretation of faith. Sociologists can explain them through population growth and social change, and we respect that. We do not say “the statistics prove God.”
2. Revivals are real, and all imperfect

In 1734 and 1735 a wave of repentance broke out in Northampton in New England. The pastor, Jonathan Edwards, wrote that the town had never been so full of love. It was part of the Great Awakening. But research from Princeton University tells us that in 1731 he bought a Black girl of about fourteen named Venus.

Let us pause. When some people read this, they want to throw Edwards away; others would rather pretend not to see it. I want to tell you that this is exactly what this lesson is after: God can truly use a person who nonetheless has huge blind spots. Revival does not make anyone a saint automatically.

Wales in 1904. A young former miner, Evan Roberts, set off a revival that swept the whole country. Many pubs fell quiet, workers brought their wages home, and miners gathered to pray before going down the shaft. Estimates of converts range from eighty thousand to a hundred and sixty thousand, a difference of a factor of two, so we should not state it with too much certainty.

And afterward? By 1906 Roberts was exhausted and withdrew from public view, spending most of the rest of his life in seclusion. Newspapers criticized him then, and even a sympathetic biographer says he sometimes believed he held powers that were not his to hold. Friends, this is not the ending of a legendary hero. This is a person who needed rest. Revival does not depend on heroes.

In 1906, Azusa Street, Los Angeles. The leader was William Seymour, whose parents had been slaves and who had lost the sight of one eye to smallpox. In the age of Jim Crow laws, he was even made to sit apart while attending classes. Yet in that humble meeting hall, Black, white and Latino worshipers prayed together. Frank Bartleman, a witness at the time, wrote that the color line had been washed away in the blood.

And then? His teacher Parham disliked the mixing of Black and white and went off to start his own meetings. Within a few years the gathering became mostly Black again. Seymour was nearly forgotten by later Pentecostal history. Today Pentecostals and charismatics are growing about 2 percent a year, one of the fastest-growing groups in Christianity, yet the line that was washed away that day was drawn back in by people.

January 1907, Pyongyang. About fifteen hundred people attended a Bible conference. Kil Sun-joo confessed his sin publicly, leading several hundred to repent together, and the tradition of early-morning prayer spread from there. The early-morning prayer tradition of Korean churches is connected with this revival. The later history of that city, everyone knows. It reminds us that revival in a place is not a permanent guarantee.

In September 1965, about two hundred people met to pray in a church on the Indonesian island of Timor, and revival began from there. It was reported at the time that between 1965 and 1967 church membership grew from 450,000 to 650,000, but that figure was later questioned. Many miracle testimonies soon spread around the world. In 1973 Christianity Today reported that investigators believed the revival was real, but that many miracles and numbers were exaggerated, and that some people joined for political reasons. Indonesia at the time was in the midst of bloody political upheaval.
The witnesses were sincere, and we believe God can do miracles. But precisely because we believe, we must check. An exaggerated testimony destroys more than one story.
The spiritual meaning: revival must begin with repentance

These stories have one thing in common: the real breakthrough often begins when someone confesses sin. The prophet Habakkuk prayed, “Renew your work in the middle of the years,” and the same verse says, “In wrath, you remember mercy.” The first beneficiary of revival should be our own conscience. In the last lesson we faced the church’s dark history, and this lesson goes on to revival; the order is right. Revival without repentance is only noise.
What does the Bible actually say?

Now we come to the key question: does the Bible promise a great revival at the end? I must be honest that brothers and sisters differ. Premillennialists mostly think the world will grow darker before the Lord returns; Jesus said, “Because iniquity will be multiplied, the love of many will grow cold,” and Paul said, “it will not be unless the rebellion comes first,” and they take these seriously. Many of them also hope for a great harvest at the same time.

Amillennialists hold that now is the age of Christ’s reign, that wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest, and that there is not necessarily one final special great revival. Postmillennialists believe the gospel will triumph greatly before the Lord returns, often citing the parable of the mustard seed, and critics think this is too optimistic about history. All three are brothers and sisters who hold to the Bible, and we respect them all.

The 321 vision is to become overcomers, move toward the great revival at the end, and welcome the Lord Jesus’ return. This is our hope and our prayer. The “last days” of Acts 2 began at Pentecost, and the promise that the Spirit is poured out on all flesh is still at work today. But we do not treat this hope as a timetable, and we do not use it to condemn others.
“But no one knows of that day and hour, not even the angels of heaven, but my Father only. (Matthew 24:36)

In church history people have kept calculating dates. In 1844 the Millerites in America believed the Lord would come that year, and many sold their farms and then waited night after night. These brothers and sisters were sincere, and the cost was heavy. The disciples also asked, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?” Jesus answered, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.” Then He turned the conversation: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.”

Remember this: the next time someone passes you an end-times timetable saying the Lord will return, or the great revival will begin, on such and such a day, you can answer with these words of Jesus, without arguing and without forwarding it.
The spiritual meaning: a grain of wheat

Finally, where does the power of revival come from? Not from our activities, not from our strategies, not from our statistics. Jesus said, “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He Himself is that grain of wheat. He died on the cross and rose on the third day. The seven hundred and fifty million in Africa and the four hundred million and more in Asia are all grains borne by that one grain of wheat.

This is also the road of selflessness. When “I” come down, Christ lives in me. Someone who wants to become famous through revival is already standing in the wrong place. “Let Jesus receive all the glory” is a sentence that has to travel from our mouths onto our calendars.

So what can we do today? First, build God’s kingdom system, starting with relationships. The 321 framework speaks of 235: spiritual companions, spiritual parents and children, and spiritual comrades in arms. Roberts’s exhaustion reminds us that revival cannot depend on one person. Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Second, send out a call to your own hometown. Many people in the world today have not heard the gospel; the Center for the Study of Global Christianity estimates that about 2.3 billion people belong to unreached peoples. The definition can be discussed, but the need is real. 544 languages are still waiting for Bible translation to begin. You do not necessarily need to go abroad; perhaps your coworker, your neighbor, your grandmother is your own ends of the earth.

Third, I want to extend an invitation to you. Will you say to the Lord today: “Lord, I do not ask for dates; revive me first”? This week list three relatives or friends who do not yet know Jesus, pray for them every day, and invite one of them to a meal. And if you have not yet believed, you are welcome to start with an honest question: if this risen Jesus is real, how would He see me?

Let us pray together. Risen Lord, Your Spirit is at work in places far beyond what I can see. Revive me first, make me humble and repentant, and free me from being the center of my own world. We do not ask for dates; we ask only to be faithful. Raise up spiritual companions and comrades in arms, build God’s kingdom system, until all peoples hear the gospel. Lord Jesus, I long for You to come! In Jesus’ name, amen.
